articles.title: Grande centro logístico em Jacareí: o que muda para quem procura imóvel | G1
articles.standfirst: Centro de distribuição do Mercado Livre, previsto para 2027 no Jardim Esperança, deve gerar cerca de 5 mil empregos. A Amagai Imóveis explica os reflexos no mercado imobiliário.
articles.summary: Centro de distribuição do Mercado Livre, previsto para 2027 no Jardim Esperança, deve gerar cerca de 5 mil empregos. A Amagai Imóveis explica os reflexos no mercado imobiliário.
articles.body:
Quando uma grande empresa de logística escolhe uma cidade, o efeito não fica restrito ao terreno onde ela se instala. O centro de distribuição do Mercado Livre em Jacareí, com conclusão prevista para 2027 e investimento estimado em R$ 500 milhões, é um exemplo. Segundo informações divulgadas pela Prefeitura de Jacareí, o empreendimento no Jardim Esperança, na região oeste, deve gerar cerca de 5 mil empregos diretos e indiretos quando estiver em operação.

Para a Amagai Imóveis, imobiliária em Jacareí , um investimento desse porte costuma movimentar o mercado imobiliário em três frentes: empresas que chegam junto, pessoas que vêm trabalhar e proprietários que passam a ver a cidade como lugar para investir. A seguir, o que cada grupo pode esperar.

Segundo Augusto Takeshi Amagai, corretor de imóveis da Amagai Imóveis (CRECI-SP 296847), a instalação de grandes operações logísticas pode gerar novas demandas por imóveis comerciais e residenciais. A avaliação dessas oportunidades, no entanto, depende das necessidades de cada empresa e da movimentação efetiva do mercado.

Por que grandes empresas escolhem Jacareí

Jacareí está no Vale do Paraíba, no eixo entre São Paulo e Rio de Janeiro. A cidade é cortada pela rodovia Presidente Dutra, tem acesso ao corredor Ayrton Senna e Carvalho Pinto e se liga à região de Campinas pela Dom Pedro I. Para uma operação que recebe e despacha caminhões todos os dias, essa combinação de rodovias pesa mais do que qualquer outro fator.

Conforme comunicado da Prefeitura de Jacareí, o projeto do centro de distribuição reúne os seguintes números e características:

Localização no Jardim Esperança, com acesso fácil às rodovias Presidente Dutra e Carvalho Pinto.

Área total de 300 mil metros quadrados e área construída estimada em 140 mil metros quadrados.

Investimento estimado em R$ 500 milhões.

Primeiro pilar instalado em 2 de junho de 2026 e conclusão prevista para 2027.

A mesma lógica vale para empresas menores. Antes de fechar um endereço em Jacareí, a equipe da Amagai orienta conferir o trajeto de chegada, os retornos e as condições de entrada e manobra dos veículos usados na operação.

Obras do centro de distribuição, em registro divulgado em junho de 2026 — Foto: Prefeitura de Jacareí

Empresas de apoio procuram galpões e salas comerciais

Uma operação logística desse tamanho não funciona sozinha. Transportadoras, fornecedores de embalagem, empresas de manutenção e prestadores de serviço tendem a procurar espaço perto da operação. É esse grupo que mais procura galpões comerciais em Jacareí e imóveis comerciais em Jacareí para alugar nos meses que antecedem a abertura de uma unidade.

A Amagai atende essas empresas a partir da operação: qual é a atividade, qual metragem é necessária e em quanto tempo a empresa precisa começar a trabalhar. Com essas informações, a equipe seleciona galpões para alugar em Jacareí , salas e pontos comerciais, e organiza as visitas com os responsáveis pela operação, para identificar adaptações antes da assinatura do contrato.

Quem precisa de um terreno para construir a própria estrutura pode avaliar o Brasporto Condomínio Empresarial , comercializado pela Amagai no bairro Rio Abaixo. O projeto tem 75 lotes, terrenos a partir de 1.000 metros quadrados e módulos adaptáveis ao tamanho da operação.

Um grande centro de distribuição atrai transportadoras, fornecedores e prestadores de serviço — e todos eles precisam de um endereço.

Quem vem trabalhar precisa de um lugar para morar

Cerca de 5 mil empregos diretos e indiretos significam também novos moradores e famílias que mudam de bairro para ficar mais perto do trabalho. A procura por casas para alugar em Jacareí e por apartamentos tende a crescer, sobretudo em bairros com acesso rápido à região oeste e à Dutra.

A Amagai tem casas e apartamentos para compra e locação em Jacareí e em São José dos Campos. Para quem está chegando à cidade, informar o local de trabalho, o orçamento e o tamanho da família ajuda a equipe a montar uma lista de imóveis para visitar. A locação pode ser feita com fiador, seguro-fiança, título de capitalização ou garantidora, o que facilita para quem ainda não tem vínculos em Jacareí.

Proprietários e investidores: imóvel para renda

Mais empresas e mais moradores também interessam a quem já tem imóvel na cidade ou pensa em comprar um para alugar. Casas, apartamentos e galpões bem localizados tendem a ficar menos tempo vagos quando a demanda cresce.

Quem tem um imóvel em Jacareí e quer colocá-lo para alugar ou vender pode falar com a equipe da Amagai para avaliar o valor e as condições de anúncio.

Amagai Imóveis atende empresas e moradores em Jacareí

A Amagai Imóveis é uma imobiliária em Jacareí com atendimento também em São José dos Campos. A carteira reúne imóveis residenciais e comerciais para compra e locação: galpões, salas e pontos comerciais, terrenos em condomínio empresarial, casas e apartamentos. A chegada de uma grande empresa de logística movimenta todas essas frentes, e a Amagai atende cada uma delas.

Os interessados podem falar com a equipe da Amagai para consultar os imóveis disponíveis e organizar visitas. O atendimento em Jacareí está disponível pelo telefone e WhatsApp (12) 3954 5000

articles.title: Governo Lula não quer transformar em crise ajuda da Casa Branca para fuga de Flávio Bolsonaro | G1
articles.standfirst: Avaliação é que Democratas já vão cobrar quem pagou avião, e Trump tem pela frente as eleições de meio de mandato. Em novembro, estarão em disputa todas as 435 cadeiras da Câmara e 35 das 100 do Senado.
articles.summary: Avaliação é que Democratas já vão cobrar quem pagou avião, e Trump tem pela frente as eleições de meio de mandato. Em novembro, estarão em disputa todas as 435 cadeiras da Câmara e 35 das 100 do Senado.
articles.body:
O presidente brasileiro Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva gesticula enquanto fala com repórteres após sua reunião na Casa Branca com o presidente dos EUA, Donald Trump, na Embaixada do Brasil em Washington, DC, EUA, em 7 de maio de 2026 — Foto: REUTERS/Elizabeth Frantz

Depois de revelado que um funcionário da Casa Branca contratou o avião da fuga de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) para os Estados Unidos , diplomatas e assessores diretos do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) avaliam que o melhor caminho é o do pragmatismo, evitando transformar o episódio em uma crise com o presidente Donald Trump.

A avaliação, inclusive, é que Trump já está sofrendo pressão e cobrança interna pela ajuda na fuga do candidato derrotado do PL, que deve crescer ainda mais diante da pergunta sobre quem pagou o jatinho contratado por Jason Miller, assessor do presidente americano na Casa Branca.

Se foi o governo dos Estados Unidos, os democratas vão usar essa informação com munição extra na eleição da semana que vem para renovação do Congresso americano. Trump deve perder maioria na Câmara dos Representantes, e corre o risco de ficar também minoria no Senado.

Será uma oportunidade para o brasileiro informar o americano que até o PL, partido de Flávio Bolsonaro, reconheceu a vitória do presidente Lula na eleição do último domingo.

Em dezembro, será a vez de Lula se encontrar com Trump na reunião dos chefes de Estado do G20.

A equipe do presidente brasileiro lembra que o americano ainda tem dois anos de mandato pela frente e o Brasil precisa conviver com ele e fazer negociações que possam beneficiar as empresas brasileiras.

articles.title: Flávio Bolsonaro: isolamento político em Brasília | G1
articles.standfirst: Postura adotada após o resultado eleitoral, questionamentos sobre as urnas e discurso de perseguição política contribuíram para o desgaste do senador entre lideranças partidárias.
articles.summary: Flávio Bolsonaro perde apoio de aliados e enfrenta isolamento político após radicalizar seu discurso e questionar a legitimidade do processo eleitoral brasileiro.
articles.body:
O senador Flávio Bolsonaro ( PL ), derrotado na disputa pela Presidência, deixou as urnas com quase 60 milhões de votos. Mas o expressivo desempenho eleitoral não foi suficiente para preservar sua força política: em apenas três dias, o parlamentar viu parte de seu apoio se dissipar. Em Brasília, a avaliação é de que suas decisões e declarações após o resultado contribuíram para seu crescente isolamento, inclusive entre lideranças partidárias e aliados do próprio campo político .

Apesar de ter demonstrado força e capacidade de articulação durante a disputa eleitoral, reunindo apoios importantes tanto no primeiro quanto no segundo turno, Flávio passou a adotar posições que provocaram desconforto entre seus aliados.

Um dos primeiros fatores de desgaste foi a resistência em reconhecer o resultado das urnas. O processo eleitoral transcorreu normalmente, com respeito às regras democráticas e à decisão da maioria. As mesmas urnas que garantiram a vitória de Flávio no primeiro turno e de seus irmãos em outras disputas passaram a ser questionadas após o resultado desfavorável.

Inicialmente, aliados tentaram contestar a prorrogação do horário de votação, medida que também havia sido solicitada pelo próprio PL. Como o impacto da mudança foi considerado pequeno, a estratégia acabou sendo modificada.

Posteriormente, os questionamentos passaram a envolver o suposto abuso do poder econômico e político por parte de quem havia sido reeleito, por meio de uma ação apresentada ao Tribunal Superior Eleitoral .

A questão, entretanto, não se limita ao campo jurídico. O reconhecimento de uma derrota eleitoral também é um gesto político, e a maior parte dos partidos demonstrou disposição para aceitar o resultado e se afastar de discursos de contestação.

Outro episódio que agravou o desgaste foi a fuga de Flávio Bolsonaro. Enquanto se apresentava como vítima de perseguição política, a avaliação feita no debate é de que sua saída estaria relacionada ao receio de uma possível prisão no contexto de uma investigação por lavagem de dinheiro que envolve seu amigo, Willer Tomaz .

A carta divulgada posteriormente também contribuiu para ampliar o constrangimento político . O documento foi considerado por aliados como um episódio particularmente problemático, sobretudo por causa do tom da primeira versão, na qual Flávio se apresentava como presidente eleito. A redação precisou ser modificada, diante da repercussão negativa e do caráter considerado absurdo da declaração.

A sequência desses acontecimentos criou um ambiente de desconforto entre os partidos. Lideranças políticas, conhecidas pelo pragmatismo, passaram a evitar o envolvimento com o discurso de Flávio. Parlamentares querem preservar suas atividades e interesses políticos, sem assumir o custo de participar de conflitos que não lhes tragam benefícios.

Flávio Bolsonaro desembarca em aeroporto próximo de Miami em 28 de outubro de 2026 — Foto: REUTERS/Eva Marie Uzcategui

A própria postura de Valdemar Costa Neto , presidente do PL, foi mencionada como exemplo desse pragmatismo. Em sua declaração, ele demonstrou que a contestação eleitoral não representava necessariamente um problema para o partido, que já havia enfrentado uma multa superior a R$ 20 milhões por questionamentos relacionados às urnas. Ainda assim, o comportamento de Flávio passou a produzir um distanciamento político.

O principal problema, portanto, é o afastamento de partidos que identificaram em seu discurso uma postura radical. Para conquistar o poder no Brasil, é necessário construir maiorias, e essas maiorias, em geral, não se identificam com posições extremadas.

Nesse contexto, Flávio Bolsonaro teria tentado reproduzir a imagem de um Bolsonaro moderado, estratégia que anteriormente havia contribuído para ampliar a votação e conquistar apoio político. Entretanto, ao adotar o discurso de contestação, associar-se a episódios de confronto institucional e assumir uma postura considerada radical, acabou se afastando dessa imagem.

O resultado é um enfraquecimento de sua posição política e a perda de espaço entre lideranças que, embora possam compartilhar parte de seu campo ideológico, preferem evitar conflitos e preservar suas próprias articulações. A fuga, a carta e o discurso adotado após o resultado eleitoral acabaram, assim, aprofundando o isolamento de Flávio Bolsonaro em Brasília.

articles.title: Sistema distrital misto: Hugo Motta quer votar mudança ainda neste ano | G1
articles.standfirst: Mudança interessa a partidos com força nos municípios e pode reduzir efeito dos “puxadores de votos”; PT e PL resistem à proposta
articles.summary: O presidente da Câmara, Hugo Motta, articula a votação do sistema distrital misto para reduzir o peso de puxadores de votos, apesar da resistência de PT e PL.
articles.body:
Parte dos parlamentares da Câmara dos Deputados quer aproveitar a atual composição da Casa para aprovar mudanças nas regras eleitorais ainda neste fim de ano. A articulação ocorre em meio à discussão sobre a adoção do sistema distrital misto, que pode alterar a forma de escolha dos deputados e reduzir a influência dos chamados puxadores de votos.

O presidente da Câmara, Hugo Motta ( Republicanos ), é favorável à proposta, que também conta com o apoio de partidos do Centrão, especialmente do PSD , liderado por Gilberto Kassab.

🔎No modelo distrital misto, o eleitor participa de uma eleição que combina duas formas de escolha: candidatos disputam vagas diretamente nos distritos, pelo sistema majoritário, e outras cadeiras são definidas conforme a votação em listas previamente organizadas pelos partidos.

🔎 Já no sistema proporcional atual, o desempenho eleitoral do partido e de seus candidatos determina quantas vagas a legenda terá no Legislativo, por meio do quociente eleitoral. Depois, essas cadeiras ficam com os candidatos mais votados da sigla.

Hugo Motta reúne presidentes de partidos para tratar de mudança no sistema eleitoral — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

Entre os principais interessados na mudança estão partidos que perderam cadeiras ou tiveram crescimento pouco expressivo nas últimas eleições. Essas legendas observam o avanço de siglas que se beneficiam do atual sistema proporcional, como o PL , que ampliou sua presença no Congresso graças, em parte, à votação expressiva de alguns candidatos.

Partidos como PSD e MDB , que possuem forte presença nos municípios e comandam diversas prefeituras, também enxergam vantagens no modelo distrital misto. Nesse sistema, a disputa é dividida por distritos eleitorais, o que pode ampliar a influência dos prefeitos na escolha dos candidatos que concorrerão às vagas de deputado.

Atualmente, o sistema proporcional permite que candidatos com votação expressiva ajudem a eleger outros integrantes de suas legendas. Conhecidos como puxadores de votos, esses parlamentares conseguem ampliar a representação partidária ao contribuir para que a sigla alcance o quociente eleitoral e partidário necessário para conquistar mais cadeiras.

Nas últimas eleições, pouco mais de 30 deputados ajudaram a eleger outros parlamentares. Ao todo, cerca de 60 candidatos teriam conquistado uma vaga beneficiados pela votação de nomes mais populares.

O fenômeno ganhou projeção nacional com Tiririca, eleito em 2010 com uma votação expressiva. Na época, sua votação ajudou a eleger outros candidatos e chamou a atenção dos partidos para o potencial desse mecanismo.

Atualmente, o cenário é diferente. As redes sociais ampliaram a capacidade de alguns políticos de mobilizar eleitores em todo o estado, transformando nomes populares no ambiente digital em importantes cabos eleitorais de suas próprias legendas. Nicolas Ferreira é um dos exemplos desse fenômeno.

A possibilidade de mudar as regras também provoca resistência entre partidos que se beneficiam do atual modelo. PT e PL estão entre as principais siglas contrárias à alteração, justamente porque possuem parlamentares com grande capacidade de mobilização eleitoral.

O debate também envolve mudanças nas regras de propaganda política nas redes sociais, outro tema que deve entrar na pauta dos parlamentares no fim do ano.

Uma das alternativas discutidas seria estabelecer um limite para a votação considerada válida para efeito de transferência de votos, evitando que candidatos com desempenho eleitoral muito acima da média ampliem excessivamente a bancada de seus partidos. Uma das hipóteses mencionadas seria estabelecer uma trava de até um milhão de votos para os chamados puxadores.

Apesar da articulação para aprovar a proposta ainda neste ano, a resistência de PT e PL, duas das principais forças políticas do país em número de votos, pode dificultar o avanço da mudança. No caso do PT, a existência de uma federação partidária também é um fator que torna a discussão mais complexa.

articles.title: Nancy Pelosi calls Mamdani, El-Sayed's past comments on Israel 'concerning' and 'wrong'
articles.summary: Nancy Pelosi called New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed's views on Israel "wrong" and not reflective of House Democrats.
articles.body:
Former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi , D-Calif., criticized New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed over their views on Israel Thursday, calling their positions "wrong" and saying they did not reflect congressional Democrats.

The two progressive Democrats were mentioned by " On Brand " podcast host Donny Deutsch, who asked Pelosi how he, as a Jewish man, could reconcile his support for the Democratic Party with politicians whose statements he considered antisemitic.

"When you say Israel doesn't have the right to be a Jewish state , that's antisemitic as far as I'm concerned with all that," Deutsch said.

When Pelosi asked for examples, Deutsch named Mamdani and El-Sayed , calling their comments "concerning."

"No, it's more than concerning," Pelosi responded. "It's wrong. It's wrong. And it isn't a reflection of the Democrats in the Congress of the United States. This new person in Michigan, we'll see if he gets elected to the Congress. But the mayor, bless his heart, I hope he succeeds as mayor, but I don't agree with some of the things he has said. But in terms of our people in the House of Representatives, if somebody says that, the other members disassociate themselves from it."

Before he was elected New York City mayor, Mamdani repeatedly dodged questions when asked if Israel should be a Jewish state. In a June 28 interview with ABC News, however, Mamdani said he supported Israel as a state with equal rights but declined to endorse it as a Jewish state.

"I think any state that privileges one religion over the other is one that I can't tell you I support, whether it be Israel or Saudi Arabia or anywhere else," Mamdani said.

El-Sayed has repeatedly declined to affirm whether Israel has the right to exist as a Jewish state. In a May appearance with Jewish supporters, the candidate said he "struggled" to answer this question and suggested the idea of a Jewish state wasn't consistent with the liberal values "we say we believe in here in the United States."

Earlier in the interview with Deutsch, Pelosi initially denied that anyone in the Democratic Party was antisemitic.

"The fact is that I really do not know of anybody there on our side who is engaged in antisemitism . That may be what it appears to be or what they're charged to be. But if they are, it's only a few. If there are, I think sometimes they say things that they shouldn't and can be interpreted that way," Pelosi said.

Despite her concerns about Mamdani and El-Sayed's comments, she dismissed their impact on the party as a whole.

"People represent their districts, and we have to respect that. The job description, job title is representative, but that doesn't mean it has an impact on the consensus of the Democratic Party, and [House Minority Leader] Hakeem Jeffries has been very clear on that," Pelosi said.

Fox News Digital reached out to representatives for Pelosi, Mamdani and El-Sayed for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

Rabbi Yaakov Menken, executive vice president of the Coalition for Jewish Values, acknowledged Pelosi "as one of the Jewish community's best friends among House Democrats" but said it was alarming that she did not seem to recognize antisemitism among her colleagues.

"Pelosi claims she wants for those voices to be marginalized within her party, yet she demonstrates that she has turned a deaf ear, both to antisemitic expression from her colleagues and to the rabbis anxious to set her straight on the magnitude of the problem. If she is indeed one of our best friends, should we not be scared by that?" Menken told Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Trump cancels weekend rallies in Iowa and Kansas in favor of holding numerous tele-rallies
articles.summary: Senate races in both states are considered toss-ups and could be key in either party’s path to control of Congress.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump announced Thursday he is canceling his rallies in Kansas and Iowa this weekend, where he had been set to stump for GOP candidates in competitive races, opting instead to do tele-rallies.

The rallies were to have been part of his planned midterm blitz, in which he said he would travel to 35 places across the country to help raise turnout for Republican candidates.

Trump has repeatedly touted what he believes is the positive impact of his rallies on GOP candidates, going as far as to suggest that his presence in battleground states has boosted Republicans in the polls.

But his tune appeared to change Thursday after his cancellations. Trump said he didn't "feel I have to go to Kansas," adding that he thinks Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, who's locked in a tight race with Democrat Adam Hamilton, "is doing well."

Concerns over high costs connected to the Iran war have helped turn the race into a toss-up in a state that hasn't sent a Democrat to the Senate for nearly a century.

Trump, who has campaigned at 25 rallies in the past month, has admitted that the blitz has not been "easy," saying through a hoarse voice Monday that "God didn't make your vocal cords to do a rally every day."

But he insisted Thursday that he felt "perfect" and lashed out at a reporter who pressed him about whether the rally cancellation in Kansas was tied to his health.

"You've been following me for two weeks. I feel perfect. You are disgusting. Put yourself in shape. You look like hell," Trump said to the journalist.

He canceled in Iowa hours after that interaction, after a White House official and a person familiar confirmed that Trump's appearance was off.

The Republican National Committee said in a news release that the rallies were canceled with the goal of "maximizing opportunities for President Donald J. Trump to speak to voters across the country."

GOP operatives in Iowa, where all congressional races this year except one are competitive, told NBC News that in-person rallies would have been helpful. Trump's rally Saturday would have been in Dubuque, in the contested 2nd Congressional District.

"A tele-rally will be helpful in boosting turnout, but an in-person rally would have been really helpful," an operative said.

Another operative said he "would love to have the president," but he said, "Iowa's in pretty good shape."

Trump is aiming to hold "more than 20" tele-rallies by Election Day, two White House officials said Thursday.

He is still scheduled to hold an event in Daytona Beach, Florida, on Friday. He will be campaigning for Republican Rep. Randy Fine and Sen. Ashley Moody, who are running in races rated solidly Republican by the nonpartisan Cook Political Report.

No events have been announced for Monday.

articles.title: US midterms: 4 days to go – What the polls say as Trump cancels two rallies
articles.summary: Trump cancels Kansas and Iowa rallies, opting for telephone events across nearly 20 states over the weekend.
articles.body:
With four days to go before the United States midterm elections , Democrats are leading in national polls as both parties make their final push for votes.

Meanwhile, a legal dispute threatens to delay the Senate result in Alaska , and President Donald Trump has cancelled two weekend rallies in favour of campaigning by phone.

What do the latest US midterm polls say?

Democrats lead Republicans by 51.4 percent to 43.2 percent, according to RealClearPolling, with a difference of 8.2 percentage points.

Charles Franklin, professor of law and public policy and director of the Marquette Law School Poll in the US, said Trump’s declining approval ratings and economic concerns are alarming Republicans.

The latest Marquette Law School poll, conducted in Wisconsin from October 14 to October 22 and released on October 28, put Trump’s approval rating at 37 percent and disapproval at 61 percent.

Only 16 percent of respondents said they were better off financially than a year ago, while 42 percent said they were worse off and another 42 percent said things were about the same.

“Democrats are more enthusiastic and more certain they will vote,” Franklin told Al Jazeera.

“That is giving Democrats an important edge, and reflects Republican disappointment in current national conditions,” he added.

In Arizona, where voters are experiencing increasing living expenses, a retiree told Al Jazeera that the cost of groceries had become a major concern.

“We’re retired, and every time we go to the grocery store, it makes me wonder what the heck is going on,” the voter said.

In Texas, Democrat James Talarico is polling at 49 percent against Republican Ken Paxton’s 43 percent, according to a CNN survey released on Thursday. In Michigan, the same pollster found Democrat Abdul El-Sayed ahead of Republican Mike Rogers, 49 percent to 42 percent.

However, Franklin warned: “Polls are not perfect predictions of outcomes.

“We could see those close races go either way, either due to polling errors or due to voters moving just a little more in one direction or the other.”

In Alaska, however, there is also a complication: a legal dispute that could delay the result of a Senate race.

What is happening in Alaska’s Senate race?

The battle for Alaska’s seat could continue in court after ballots close on November 3. The dispute centres on two candidates named Dan Sullivan : the incumbent Republican senator and an independent candidate with the same name, who is also registered as a Republican.

Trump has accused Democrats of recruiting an independent candidate to confuse voters and take support away from the Republican senator.

“It was a scheme. It was an election fraud. Total election fraud,” Trump said.

The Justice Department has taken legal action over the dispute, while Democrat Mary Peltola denied the accusations.

“I feel like this is yet another diversion from the issue that Alaskans want to talk about, which is affordability,” she said.

Al Jazeera’s US correspondent Alan Fisher said the dispute could have consequences beyond Alaska if the Senate’s control depends on the result.

“If this becomes the key seat in the battle for the Senate, we might not actually know who has control there for several days, maybe even weeks after November 3,” Fisher said.

What has happened on the campaign trail in the past 24 hours?

Trump travelled to South Carolina to campaign for Republican senator Darline Graham – sister of the late Lindsey Graham – who is running against Annie Andrews in a closely contested race.

In Rock Hill, Trump encouraged voters to cast their ballots and cautioned his supporters not to take the election outcome for granted. About Graham, Trump said that she was in the lead but that he still had to campaign there. “In politics you never know, right? So you got to get out and vote.”

He also addressed his supporters directly and asked the crowd to pretend that he was on the ballot.

“And I am on the ballot because all of these things that we’ve done, all of these incredible successes that we have,” he added.

In Texas, Vice President JD Vance attended a rally in Weatherford, near Dallas, alongside Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton, as Republicans called on supporters to vote.

“Texas ain’t surrendering. Texas is not becoming California. It’s going to stay Texas, ain’t that right?” Vance told supporters.

Well-known Democrats have also joined the campaign trail.

On Wednesday, former President Barack Obama gave a speech in Georgia supporting Senator Jon Ossoff, criticising Trump’s management of the economy and his approach to the war with Iran.

When Al Jazeera asked about Obama’s visit, Ossoff’s Republican opponent, Mike Collins, said it showed “the desperation of Jon Ossoff because he knows he’s losing”.

“If he was winning so big, he wouldn’t have brought anybody in,” Collins said.

Democrats also campaigned in Texas and Georgia on Thursday.

In Dallas, Senate candidate James Talarico held a rally as part of his final campaign tour, while former Vice President Kamala Harris joined Ossoff at Clark Atlanta University, urging young people to vote.

Harris also campaigned in Macon, Georgia, where she criticised the Trump administration over rising living costs.

“We have a moment now to turn pain into purpose,” Harris told Democratic volunteers. Harris also urged supporters to participate in local and statewide contests.

Later, at Clark Atlanta University, she asked students to stay engaged.

“Don’t overlook those races, because those are the folks who make decisions about your life every day,” she said.

What happens next on the US midterms campaign trail?

Trump has cancelled weekend scheduled appearances in Kansas and Iowa, replacing them with telephone rallies across nearly 20 states in the final days before Tuesday’s elections.

Trump had been set to appear in Salina, Kansas, on Saturday and Dubuque, Iowa, on Sunday .

Republican National Committee Chairman Joe Gruters said the change would allow Trump to reach more voters than he could with in-person appearances.

“Voters across the country want to hear from President Trump before Election Day, and this 72-hour sprint will be a huge boost in the closing days,” Gruters said.

Asked about the cancellations on Thursday, Trump questioned the need to travel to Kansas, where Republican Senator Roger Marshall is facing Democrat Adam Hamilton.

“I don’t feel I have to go to Kansas,” Trump said.

When a Reuters reporter asked whether the decision had anything to do with fatigue from travelling, Trump rejected the suggestion. “I feel perfect,” he said, before insulting the reporter.

Trump is still scheduled to hold a rally at the Ocean Center in Daytona Beach, Florida, on Friday at 23:00 GMT.

At the same time, Harris is due to address the Fulton County Democratic Party’s Fulton Forward dinner in Atlanta, Georgia.

Vance had also planned a news conference with the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud in St Cloud, Minnesota, on Friday, but the visit was cancelled on Thursday. No reason was immediately given.

articles.title: ‘We just have to bother the crap out of these people’: How the GOP is confronting its voter enthusiasm deficit
articles.summary: For Republicans, the midterm alarm bells are increasingly coming from inside their house.
articles.body:
For Republicans, the midterm alarm bells are increasingly coming from inside their house.

In Georgia, Rick Jackson, the GOP nominee for governor, has expressed concerns that rural voters had grown complacent. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis described turnout in his state as underwhelming and said, "Republicans have some work to do." And in Texas, Bo French, the conservative firebrand running to be the state's powerful railroad commissioner, has taken to social media to call out Republicans – especially men – in the counties he says are lagging behind Democrats.

"Get off the bench," French wrote this week . "The other side is showing up."

Across the country, in blue states and red, in marquee races and down-ballot contests, Republicans are confronting an unsettling reality: Democrats are showing a surge in enthusiasm their own party has struggled to match.

A recent CNN/SSRS survey found 61% of registered voters who are leaning Democrat this year are extremely motivated to vote, up significantly from 34% four years ago . Meanwhile, Republican enthusiasm has barely budged since the last midterm election. CNN/SSRS polls in the battleground states of Texas, Kansas, Michigan and Maine found Democrats hold a significant edge in likely voters that are highly motivated .

Republican voters are also less likely than Democrats to say it matters which party wins the House of Representatives in November, according to Pew Research polls . And while they were more attuned to the election than Democrats four years ago, the sentiments have flipped heading into November.

One Republican National Committee official acknowledged the uphill climb facing the party. The official, who asked not to be named to discuss the midterm strategy, said Republicans have a tougher task than Democrats. They must sell voters on President Donald Trump's accomplishments amid intensifying economic concerns, while also convincing them a Democratic takeover of Congress would be worse.

"That's harder than saying, 'Orange man bad,'" the official said.

Christina Crosby, chairwoman for the local Republican Party in Durham County, North Carolina, said Republicans in Washington haven't adequately communicated the president's accomplishments to voters in her state, where a US Senate seat is up for grabs. With just days remaining until the votes are counted, she said the outcome remains "hard to read" but she senses a broader weariness among the public.

"There's a fatigue across America with this political divide and I feel like there are people on both sides who are saying they're throwing up their hands at all the texts and ads and saying, 'I don't want any more of this,'" she said. "It's making it harder to get people out to the polls across the board. But the uneducated voter is the most dangerous thing."

The challenge mobilizing Trump's coalition

From the moment Trump returned to the White House, Republicans have maneuvered to overcome the historical headwinds that face the party in power and the challenge of keeping his voters engaged without him on the ballot.

Trump's political operation and Republican fundraising gave the party an unprecedented financial edge over Democrats. Meanwhile, Trump and his advisers ignited a mid-decade redistricting war intended to boost their chances of keeping the House.

But those efforts now confront a political climate far more hostile than Republicans anticipated. An unpopular war, high gas prices, widespread economic unease and Trump's sinking approval rating have threatened to overwhelm the advantages created by hundreds of millions of dollars of ad spending and a favorable electoral map.

Perhaps the clearest evidence of the enthusiasm gap presenting itself at the ballot box so far is Democrats' success turning out voters who might otherwise sit out a midterm election. In Kansas and North Carolina, for example, Democrats have opened large leads among voters who didn't vote in one or both of the last two elections, according to a CNN analysis of early voting data .

If that advantage holds — far from a guarantee — it could prove a consequential reversal of two years ago when Trump won every battleground state and the popular vote in part by picking up new support from Americans who rarely participate in elections.

Hilario Deleon, chairman of the Republican Party in Milwaukee County, said his organization has spent much of the last two years focused on reaching the new voters that Trump turned out. While he believes they've made headway, he also acknowledged that many remain unaware of the stakes this November and why their involvement is even needed.

"Politics is secondary and I don't blame them for turning on a sports game to get a break from the world," Deleon said. "It's not necessarily that they're angry at the president. But you're going to find most people just don't understand why it's so important to show up in a midterm cycle."

It's relatively new for Republicans to have to hound people on their side to cast ballots. Trump's unique appeal in communities that tend to vote blue or not at all has transformed the party's coalition, but it has also left Republicans struggling to replicate his success outside of presidential elections. Groups like Turning Point USA , the organization founded by the late conservative activist Charlie Kirk, have recalibrated to create large ballot chasing operations to track down these irregular voters, but it remains a work in progress.

"We've had several cycles to learn how to do it and there's definitely a learning curve," said Danedri Herbert, the GOP chairwoman in Kansas, the site of an unexpectedly competitive Senate race. "Democrats have been good at that for a long time, but we're catching up to them."

The RNC official said the challenge can be as basic as informing voters when the election is taking place.

"We just have to bother the crap out of these people to get them to vote," the official said. "We're talking 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 times to get them to action."

Despite the troubling early indicators, some Republicans see reason for optimism heading into the final days.

Herbert said any angst she felt looking at early voting returns a week ago has largely subsided and given way to confidence that the math is on her side. In Kansas, there are nearly 400,000 more registered Republicans than Democrats and she believes there are already indications they are making their presence felt.

Republican gains in voter registration in recent years, particularly in key battlegrounds, have strengthened the party's position heading into the midterms , offering a potential counterweight to the Democrats' enthusiasm advantage.

"Republicans are coming home, and they're coming home fast," she said. "I definitely feel a vibe shift."

Republicans are also counting on Trump's aggressive travel schedule to help mobilize their side. For months, Trump has urged Republicans to vote as if he's on the ballot. (Democrats, for their part, have long argued that Trump also motivates their voters wherever he goes.)

Doug Deeken, chairman of the Wayne County Republican Party in Ohio, said voters in his northeast corner of the state are responding to the message. Trump and Vice President JD Vance have made multiple visits to the state as Republicans face exceptionally competitive races for Senate and governor.

"If the president only had time to visit Michigan and Texas, maybe that would have worried me," Deeken said. "But they're spreading the love around."

Deeken said Republicans in his county are outpacing their 2022 performance. To him, it's a sign that the polls are missing quiet Republican voters and that conventional wisdom about midterms may not apply to an election as unusual as the second midterm of a norm-busting president serving nonconsecutive terms.

"Every time we think we know how politics works, especially in the era of Donald Trump, it changes," he said. "People are trying to apply old rules to a new day."

CNN's Edward Wu and Ariel Edwards-Levy contributed to this report.

articles.title: Resurfaced Peltola 'criminal offense' quote comes back to haunt her after explosive report: 'Turn yourself in'
articles.summary: Mary Peltola faces social media criticism after a resurfaced quote clashes with a New York Times report on spoiler candidates in the Alaska Senate race.
articles.body: Alaska Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola is facing an onslaught of social media criticism over a resurfaced quote that critics say reeks of hypocrisy, following an explosive New York Times report this week. "It should be a criminal offense to lie or mislead the electorate," Peltola says in the clip from August posted by the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC) on Wednesday, shortly after The New York Times reported that her campaign was actively involved in a scheme to peel votes away from incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan by recruiting namesake and spoiler candidates. Conservatives on social media quickly shared the post and suggested that Peltola should be investigated based on her own words. "Your terms are acceptable," Townhall columnist Dustin Grage posted on X. MARY PELTOLA'S CAMPAIGN, DEMS BACKED COVERT SCHEME TO FIELD SPOILER CANDIDATES IN ALASKA SENATE RACE: REPORT "Turn yourself in, Mary Peltola," conservative radio host Jason Rantz posted on X. "Amen, Mary! " former Trump campaign national press secretary Hogan Gidley posted on X. "Well, that’s ironic… ," Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., posted on X. "Agree!!! " Fox News contributor Marc Thiessen posted on X. ALASKA'S GOVERNOR ORDERS INVESTIGATION AFTER NYT REPORT ON ALLEGED DEM-LINKED SENATE ELECTION SCHEME The New York Times report rocked the Alaska Senate race, which could determine the balance of power in the Senate, as questions now swirl over the legality of the campaign's alleged actions. The Department of Justice and the state of Alaska are both investigating the genesis of the alleged scheme to recruit Dan J. Sullivan into the race against incumbent Dan S. Sullivan. Fox News learned Wednesday that federal prosecutors are conducting an "aggressive criminal investigation" into how the second Sullivan secured a spot on Alaska's ballot, according to two sources familiar with the probe. Investigators are preparing grand jury subpoenas and examining potential violations of voters' rights, with the investigation expected to continue beyond Election Day. The DOJ declined to comment. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Alaska's Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy announced that he was ordering a probe into the matter. "Today’s New York Times reporting reveals disturbing new evidence of an organized effort to manipulate Alaska’s elections by recruiting candidates — including one with the same name as an incumbent U.S. Senator — to deliberately confuse voters and misdirect their votes. The Alaska Division of Elections investigated these very concerns in June of this year. The new reporting substantially supports the Division’s findings," Dunleavy noted in a post on X. "I am therefore directing the Department of Public Safety to investigate whether this scheme violated Alaska’s laws and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted. The evidence will determine what happens next," the GOP governor continued. The DOJ has issued dozens of subpoenas in the past 24 hours, reportedly looking into whether the campaign violated federal law by conspiring against the rights of voters. Others have argued the alleged actions are not illegal, and simply a "dirty trick" that is sometimes utilized in campaigns. Fox News Digital reached out to Peltola's campaign for comment. Peltola has dismissed reports of the alleged election scheme as "just another distraction," arguing that The New York Times’ report was solely purposed to "sell newspapers." Her campaign also continues to assert innocence, previously telling Fox News in part that the Alaskans for Mary campaign "has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign."

articles.title: James Comey team in court seeking to toss out third DOJ case against longtime Trump foe
articles.summary: Attorneys for the former FBI director contend the third case isn’t valid on its face because it wasn’t presented to a federal grand jury within the statute of limitations.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — Attorneys for former FBI Director James Comey will be in court Friday seeking to toss out the third federal criminal case the Trump administration has brought against him in the past 13 months. Comey, who has long been a target of Donald Trump’s since the president fired him nearly a decade ago, is facing a case involving two alleged crimes that date back to 2016. His attorneys contend there’s no valid case against him: The government didn’t secure an indictment from a grand jury before the statute of limitations of 10 years expired. It was the third case against Comey since September 2025, when a Trump-aligned attorney convinced a federal grand jury to return an indictment against Comey in the Eastern District of Virginia. That case was later tossed because the attorney, Lindsey Halligan, was found to have been unlawfully acting as a federal prosecutor. Then came the seashells case: A federal grand jury in the Eastern District of North Carolina indicted Comey over an Instagram photo he posted with seashells arranged to spell out “8647,” which prosecutors contended was a threat against the president. Comey’s team has moved to dismiss that case on several grounds and says the picture was clearly not intended as a threat. The term “86” is widely known in the restaurant world to mean the kitchen is out of a dish. A federal judge has not yet ruled and knocked back the trial until 2027. The latest case centers on the allegation that Comey, while FBI director in October 2016, authorized his staff to speak to a New York Times reporter to correct the record about another report that dealt with classified information. The case was brought under seal on Oct. 5, exactly 10 years after a story ran in The New York Times that discussed how Yahoo had been complying with a secret order from the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court that led to the systematic scanning of email traffic from users of its email service. The case against Comey was not the result of a grand jury indictment or a criminal complaint evaluated by a judge, but rather through a criminal information filed directly by the government, with no judge sign-off. Comey’s team believed that the government intended to secure an arrest warrant and execute an after-hours arrest on the Friday before Columbus Day weekend to ensure Comey sat in jail over a long holiday weekend. Legal experts questioned the mechanism that government attorneys used to bring the case. “They brought the case in such a way that undermines their complaint in the first place,” said former federal prosecutor Sarah Krissoff. “If they had a case, then they should have written out the charges in a complaint and gotten a judge to sign it, or they could have presented it to a grand jury.” Krissoff called the Justice Department’s handling of the situation “disturbing.” “Somebody is dictating this process, saying, ‘Bring the case,’” Krissoff said. “The case is going to go nowhere.” U.S. District Judge Trevor McFadden ordered the case unsealed Monday and set a hearing for Friday on Comey’s motion to dismiss. The Comey hearing comes at the end of a week focused on political cases in federal court in Washington, where a federal grand jury rejected the Trump administration’s attempts to indict Cassidy Hutchinson, a star witness for the House Jan. 6 committee. Separately, a federal magistrate judge held days of hearings to examine the validity of charges brought by criminal complaint against two former FBI employees who had been targeted by Trump allies on Capitol Hill. “We have grand juries that are holding tight to the rule of law and actually asking questions most likely and requiring real evidence to be presented to them,” Krissoff said. “As a citizen, I’m sitting here saying, ‘Thank goodness for the federal judiciary,’ because they’re holding our country together, in my view.”

articles.title: Trump-backed Alaska candidate blasts 'so-called Republican' Murkowski for endorsing Dem
articles.summary: Trump-backed Alaska gubernatorial candidate Bernadette Wilson slammed Sen. Lisa Murkowski for endorsing her Democratic opponent, accusing the two of sharing liberal economic policies.
articles.body: Alaska Republican gubernatorial candidate Bernadette Wilson said she was not surprised Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, crossed party lines to endorse her Democratic opponent in the governor's race. Wilson told Fox News Digital that Murkowski endorsed Democratic gubernatorial candidate Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins on Tuesday because the two share similar views on taxation and Alaska's oil industry. "It should not surprise anyone. They're two peas in a pod, and I can tell you that as governor," Wilson told Fox News Digital. FORMER STATE REP TOPS RANKED-CHOICE SLUGFEST AS ALASKA ADVANCES NOMINEES FOR GOVERNOR "It doesn't surprise me that she is supporting the just keep taxing JKT," Wilson continued. "You know the guy that supports an increase in income tax, the guy that wants to double the fuel tax here in Alaska, the guy that has said ‘Hey I’m gonna come after the oil companies,' the guy that does not support paying out a full permanent fund dividend." In August, during a candidate forum hosted by the Alaska Oil and Gas Association, Kreiss-Tomkins said he believes "broad-based tax and revenues of that nature are likely going to be necessary to balance our budget." DEM SENATE HOPEFUL VOWS TO UNLEASH ALASKA OIL — BUT HER RECORD TELLS A DIFFERENT STORY Wilson argued that Kreiss-Tomkins' economic policies align with Murkowski's, accusing both politicians of supporting what she described as "socialist policies." The Republican candidate said she has been "sounding the alarm since 2010 about the fact that she was [subscribing] to extreme liberal socialist policies," referring to Murkowski. Wilson also said she would not "assign motive" to Murkowski's decision to endorse Kreiss-Tomkins, though she did not rule out the possibility that the endorsement was intended as a rebuke of President Donald Trump. Trump endorsed Wilson on Oct. 13, days before Murkowski announced her support for Kreiss-Tomkins. Murkowski has opposed several legislative priorities backed by Trump during the 119th Congress, including the SAVE America Act, which would impose additional proof-of-citizenship requirements for voter registration. In an op-ed for The Wall Street Journal in July, Murkowski wrote that "as written, the SAVE America Act isn’t a simple fix to safeguard elections, as proponents claim. It would impose costly new barriers and prevent some, perhaps many, from voting, while also creating chaos before the November elections." JOHNSON'S STRATEGY TO BYPASS DEMOCRATS' SAVE ACT BLOCKADE SURVIVES KEY VOTE, HANDING GOP BIG WIN In January, Murkowski joined Senate Democrats in voting in favor of the War Powers Resolution, which failed but could have limited Trump’s ability to take military action against Iran. The president then took to Truth Social to state that Murkowski "should never be elected to office again." If elected governor, Wilson pledged in her video interview that she would continue to "sound the alarm" about Murkowski, whom she described as a "so-called Republican senator." The candidate also characterized Murkowski's political positions as "absolutely terrible." articles.title: Democrats demand answers from State about taking in Bolsonaro
articles.summary: They want to know if administration officials helped Bolsonaro get out of Brazil, and why he was granted a U.S. visa.
articles.body:
House Democrats are probing the State Department's role in facilitating former Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro's escape from Brazil to the U.S. amid ongoing criminal investigations into him and his family.

A group of House Democrats, including many prominent members of the Foreign Affairs Committee, sent a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Thursday night with a list of questions about the State Department's involvement in Bolsonaro fleeing Brazil and the process it underwent to approve a U.S. visa for him as he departed.

In the letter, shared first with POLITICO , the Democrats ask Rubio to clarify how the State Department coordinated with other agencies to grant the visa, whether officials were aware of the pending probes against Bolsonaro and the degree to which the State Department and its officials helped Bolsonaro leave Brazil and come to the United States.

"The American people and Congress have a legitimate oversight interest in understanding whether U.S. diplomatic and immigration resources were used to facilitate the travel of a foreign political figure under these circumstances," the lawmakers wrote. "Transparency is particularly important where the reported events implicate a foreign judicial proceeding, sensitive bilateral relations, and the consistent application of U.S. immigration and diplomatic policies."

The letter, led by Reps. Sydney Kamlager-Dove (D-Calif.) and Dina Titus (D-Nev.), was signed by 25 members in total.

The State Department did not respond to a request for comment about the letter.

Bolsonaro, the scion of a right-wing political dynasty in the South American country with close ties to key Trump administration advisers, is under investigation in Brazil for alleged money laundering. After he lost the second round of the presidential election to incumbent left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on Sunday, a Brazilian judge ordered that he surrender his passport and remain in Brazilian territory. Instead, he fled the country with his wife and children, traveling first to Argentina and then Miami.

POLITICO has not been able to independently confirm those reports. The White House directed a request for comment about administration involvement to the State Department as well as Customs and Border Protection.

The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees CBP, did not address reports of administration involvement directly, but did say in a statement that "Bolsonaro arrived in South Florida with his family and were met and inspected by U.S. Customs and Border Protection in accordance with applicable immigration laws and procedures. At the conclusion of the inspection, Mr. Bolsonaro and his accompanying family members were released."
