articles.title: Gen Z trusts elections, but not Washington
articles.summary: For younger voters, election-related corruption is less of a concern than for older generations. Four percent of Gen Zers say they’re worried about election fraud and cheating ahead of the midterms, compared with 14 percent of millennials, 21 percent of Gen Xers and 23 percent of baby boomers, per a CBS/YouGov poll. The results also…
articles.body:
For younger voters, election-related corruption is less of a concern than for older generations.

Four percent of Gen Zers say they’re worried about election fraud and cheating ahead of the midterms, compared with 14 percent of millennials, 21 percent of Gen Xers and 23 percent of baby boomers, per a CBS/YouGov poll.

The results also show that young adults are more concerned with an “unwanted election outcome.” Seventeen percent of the age group is worried about it, compared with 13 percent of millennials and Gen Xers and 11 percent of boomers.

“Generally, Gen Z does not trust D.C.,” Dakota Hall, executive director of Alliance for Youth Action (AYA), told The Hill. “Nor is trust built for them in D.C. It’s built for them down the street.”

Politicians like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) serve as a case study into young adults’ trust in local politics. His campaigns to fix potholes and basketball courts, among other things that affect New Yorkers’ everyday lives, foster confidence in the city’s political system.

Hall quoted an interview that podcaster Theo Von conducted with Mamdani. “You’re just giving people a chance to breathe,” he told the mayor.

To Hall, this concept is key to young voters.

Reports of corruption in Washington, including the Jeffrey Epstein files or President Trump’s inflated earnings while in office , muddy the waters for Generation Z.

AYA polling from October found that corruption in the political system either tied or beat jobs and the economy as a top concern for young adults in the states it surveyed.

“A lot of people view the corruption as to why they can’t get a job,” Hall said. “A lot of young people were in favor of the DOGE [Department of Government Efficiency] efforts because they thought it would even the playing field for them.”

In reality, the economic conditions have worsened as the cost of living has increased.

“Young people have the highest bulls‑‑‑ meter of all time, and they’re more informed than people believe them to be,” Hall said.

Gen Z may not be as tuned in to legacy media as older generations, but that does not make it less informed. Young adults get news on social media, including from influencers they grow to trust. This is similar to their interest in local politics: seeing familiar faces break down what’s happening and why it’s important.

Politicians are going to have to change their messaging to regain that trust, and it starts at elections.

“We have to talk like normal people,” Hall said. “That’s where Gen Z is going to make that change.”

For Dylan Hedtler‑Gaudette, who leads government affairs at the Project on Government Oversight, younger generations’ better media comprehension might explain their less prominent focus on corrupt elections.

“Younger people are a bit more competent at understanding, especially in the sort of digital space, being in social media or the traditional internet or anywhere else, how to make distinctions between actual information and bulls‑‑‑,” Hedtler‑Gaudette told The Hill.

Will Gen Z actually show up on Election Day?

Generation Z has been told that every election it has voted in is the most important one yet, but it’s getting repetitive.

Some polls have found that Gen Z is more midterms motivated than ever. An URGE and HIT Strategies survey of young voters found that 93 percent said they “will certainly” or “probably” vote in this year’s midterms.

But others, like one from Harvard University’s Kennedy School of Politics , found that Americans aged 18-29 are less enthusiastic than in previous years.

Thirty-three percent of young Americans said they plan to definitely vote in November, down from the 2018 and 2022 midterms, where 40 percent said the same. The poll also found that 50 percent of Gen Z Democrats plan to vote, compared with 34 percent of Republicans.

An analysis from the Grand Bargain Project on 2024’s voter turnout numbers looked at why fewer than half of eligible Gen Zers showed up.

“Young people care. They are highly engaged through social media and online. They do not vote because they do not think it will make any difference,” the Grand Bargain Project wrote.

“More empty promises and inspired talking points will not convince them otherwise. Generation Z is disillusioned with political pandering. It will take a new approach to bring them to the ballot box. It will take real, legitimate change.”

Some Gen Zers, like Alexander Brown, youth leadership analyst and CEO of Together!, are poised to believe that young adults now understand the value of their vote.

“Gen Z is now feeling that their voice has to translate over into electoral power,” Brown told The Hill. “We understand that the catalyst is translating that over to our vote.”

As gas and energy prices continue to climb, Gen Z may be more motivated to show up on Tuesday, as affordability is top of mind .

“Gen Z is influenced by digital trends and social media that are able to tailor to their needs. Ultimately, what Gen Z wants are things broken down into layman’s terms, to know how it will benefit them,” Brown said.

He added that in the past, a lot of issues have been used as a form of “political theater,” but the issues young adults are facing today require distinct policy change. Gen Z will show up in “droves” to elect local, state and federal leaders, Brown predicts.

“We don’t want to live a life of tough times,” he said.

One last thing: Democrats dominate the TikTok midterm algorithm

Democratic candidates dominated TikTok ahead of November’s midterms, according to Knox Digital.

Fifteen percent of Republican candidates posted on the social media platform between January and October, compared with 51 percent of Democrats. And Democrats received 76 percent of all candidate views, while the GOP received 24 percent.

TikTok is dominated by Generation Z — 56 percent of U.S. adults aged 18-24 use the platform, per Pew Research . These insights into what politicians are pouring into the platform show a sliver of how they seek out attracting younger voters.

TikTok reveals a key weakness in the GOP’s midterms communications, Knox Digital said. Attack content performs best for Democrats, but Republicans make more of those videos.

Democrats prioritized posting about corruption, including the Epstein files, the cost of living and healthcare. Republicans, meanwhile, focused on crime and policing, attacks on the other party and immigration.

Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.) and Rep. Brandon Gill (R-Texas) topped their respective parties’ TikTok takeovers. Booker received 371.8 million views and 30.8 million engagements, and Gill received 280.3 million views and 29.3 million engagements.

Knox Digital tracked TikTok accounts of 303 House and Senate candidates across 48 states, covering 31,872 videos between Jan. 1 and Oct. 23.

The Feed is a weekly scoop on Generation Z put together by three Generation Z editors at The Hill. We’re working to understand the ins and outs of our generation’s politics. Send tips or comments to awalker@thehill.com, jfeldstein@thehill.com or cleibowitz@thehill.com.

articles.title: Lingering Democratic divisions could preview 2028 challenges
articles.summary: Democrats are weeks away from the start of the next presidential primary — a contest many in the party have been eagerly anticipating since their devastating loss in the 2024 race. But the divisions that could shape the 2028 race are already on full display, even as Democrats look to make gains in the House…
articles.body:
Democrats are weeks away from the start of the next presidential primary — a contest many in the party have been eagerly anticipating since their devastating loss in the 2024 race. But the divisions that could shape the 2028 race are already on full display, even as Democrats look to make gains in the House and Senate in Tuesday’s midterm elections.

In Michigan and Texas, for example, two contentious Senate primaries have left lingering friction between the party’s nominees and their defeated rivals, months after Democrats urged both sides to put aside their differences in the interest of winning.

The rift in Michigan has been particularly striking: Rep. Haley Stevens’s (D-Mich.) fiancé publicly declared that he would vote for Republican Mike Rogers over Abdul El-Sayed, the Democrat who defeated Stevens in the Senate primary. Stevens’s former campaign chair also said he plans to vote for Rogers, although Stevens herself says she will cast a vote for her former rival, who is more progressive.

In the Lone Star State, Rep. Jasmine Crockett (D-Texas) has endorsed Texas state Rep. James Talarico, who defeated her in the Democratic Senate primary, but she has not campaigned alongside him.

The tensions offer a glimpse of the challenges awaiting a crowded field of candidates who will have to find ways of navigating their party’s ideological divides.

Some Democratic strategists worry the internal fights will spill into the presidential contest in a much more dramatic fashion than in previous presidential races.

“For sure, we’re going to relitigate the 2016 and 2020 primary all over again in 2028,” said Democratic strategist Steve Schale, who ran former President Obama’s Florida operation during his successful presidential bids. “It’s real.”

One Democratic donor added: “Anyone saying we don’t have a huge problem on our hands is in denial.”

Democratic strategist Eddie Vale said the takeaway from the midterms should be: “Everyone chill out and let’s just win, baby.”

But he said he suspects the strain may persist.

“More likely it’s the opening skirmishes of the inter-party fights everyone is gonna try and litigate endlessly until 2028,” Vale said. “But knock on wood, if they both win, it should show the different factions that there is no one magical trick to win everywhere and need the right candidates in the right places and that candidate quality matters a lot, too — not just ideology.”

In Michigan, the divisions have been pronounced.

Nearly three months after the end of a bitter primary, El-Sayed and Stevens have barely spoken since appearing together — and hugging one another — at a unity event.

CNN reported this week that conversations between the two sides “quickly dried up” after the event, and while El-Sayed’s staff picked up some of Stevens’s aides for his campaign, the two principals have not been “directly in touch.”

Jason Turkish, Stevens’s fiancé, explained Wednesday that El-Sayed’s rhetoric on Israel and Gaza led to his decision to support Rogers.

“I’ve just seen an escalation in his rhetoric since the primary, and it makes folks unsafe,” Turkish, who is Jewish and has been a critic of the Israeli government, told The Detroit News. “Every time he talks about genocide, Jews get death threats.”

Stevens, who has been campaigning for Democrat Jocelyn Benson in Michigan’s gubernatorial race, is not expected to join El-Sayed for any events in the lead-up to Election Day.

Still, she said she is supporting her former rival.

“Like a lot of households across America, we’re a house divided ,” she told CNN Wednesday. “I still very much want our Democratic nominee, his name is Abdul, to win this race.”

In the Texas Senate race, while Crockett hasn’t appeared with Talarico at recent campaign stops, she told the Houston Chronicle that she “endorsed him 100 times.”

A string of democratic socialist victories across the country this year has infused the party’s overall dynamic with discord. Those wins have Democrats, particularly moderates, concerned that the infighting will not only continue, it might get worse.

Democratic strategist Basil Smikle said it shows that “ideological and operational differences can sadly still stifle Democrats and snatch defeat out of the jaws of victory by not seeing the big picture.”

In the 2028 race, Smikle said it could spell “disaster if Democrats don’t focus on the voters and institutions and not themselves.”

“Democrats can’t get locked in an internal squabble that overcomes their ability to convince voters they should be back in the White House,” he said.

At the same time, Democratic strategist Christy Setzer said any dissension is “overstated.”

“Not saying there aren’t some hurt feelings about primary losses, but we see some version of this every election, and both Stevens and Crockett have said they’ll back the Democratic ticket,” Setzer said.

She highlighted the similar disharmony when Democrats were worried that supporters of Hillary Clinton would stay home instead of supporting Obama in the general election in 2008.

She noted Republicans have more at stake in the midterms and beyond.

“I’d be far more worried if I were Ken Paxton, trying to win over [Sen.] John Cornyn [(R-Texas)] voters, or even [Sen.] Darline Graham [(R-S.C.)], trying to court [Rep.] Ralph Norman [(R-S.C.)] voters — both who have implied they’d either sit out the race or even back the Democrat,” Setzer said of Cornyn and Norman, who were defeated in GOP primaries.

Democrats on Capitol Hill, she said, are united on economic issues including the cost of living and holding the Trump administration accountable

“Do I see this as a problem in the next Congress? Absolutely not,” Selzer said of party tension. “We have much bigger fish to fry.”

The unnamed Democratic donor said the party’s problems, which have been simmering for months this year, could reach a “boiling point” in the coming months.

“This is going to be the nastiest, most horrific primary we’ve ever seen,” the donor said.

“It’s going to be brutal, and we’re going to have to find a way to not f— this up. And based on our history, I’m not entirely sure we have the ability to not f— this up.”

articles.title: RNC rejects narrative of spoiler candidates 'on both sides,' calls Alaska scheme 'fraudulent'
articles.summary: The RNC says Democrats recruited a second Dan Sullivan onto Alaska's Senate ballot to confuse voters as the DOJ intensifies its criminal probe.
articles.body: The Republican National Committee rejected the narrative that both parties engage in similar tactics after a New York Times report exposed Democrat-linked efforts to recruit a second "Dan Sullivan" onto Alaska’s Senate ballot, saying Republicans are focused solely on securing elections while Democrats are "trying to be fraudulent." "No, both sides of the aisle don’t do this," RNC election integrity communications director Ally Triolo told Fox News Digital on Thursday. "Our entire effort here at the RNC is securing elections, making them fair and free and honest." "We are doing the exact opposite of what Democrats are trying to do. Democrats have voted time and time again against the Save America Act. They have voted against common sense safeguards. DEM STRATEGIST SHRUGS OFF ALASKA BALLOT SCANDAL ON MS NOW, INSISTS 'THIS STUFF HAPPENS ALL THE TIME' "We couldn't be more different from Republicans versus Democrats, and I honestly hope people see this straight in the eye with what's happened out of Alaska, that Democrats are completely disingenuous. They have ill intentions. They're trying to disenfranchise voters, and, of course, trying to be fraudulent. "This is fraudulent behavior, and they need to be held accountable to the fullest extent." The Times reported Wednesday that Senate nominee Mary Peltola’s campaign, aides from the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and others worked to place a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan on the ballot. JASON CHAFFETZ: DEMOCRATS TRIED TO TRICK ALASKA VOTERS. PELTOLA MUST ANSWER "Republicans, we tried to fight this months ago and draw attention to this Democrat scheme," Triolo said. "And look, no wonder Democrats are against election integrity because they don't want to be held accountable for trying to disenfranchise voters and cheat the system." "It has been abundantly clear from the get-go that this was a ploy to try to sway voters, confuse voters, take votes away from the real Sen. Dan Sullivan," she added. "And that is exactly why you saw the DOJ intervene just last week to make sure there were protections in place before the election could be certified to make sure everything was above board. And now we have this bombshell report coming out exposing exactly what we have been saying, and I think this points to the larger issue of Democrats continually fighting election integrity, because again, they have admitted that they cannot win fair and square when safeguards are in place." TRUMP SAYS 'WE ARE LOOKING INTO' OTHER DAN SULLIVAN ON ALASKA BALLOT, WARNS ABOUT GOVERNOR'S RACE The RNC election integrity unit has a major on-the-ground operation in Alaska, she said, including an in-state director, attorneys, observers and poll workers, and that President Donald Trump and the Justice Department have already moved to address the issue. The DOJ last week sued to block certification of a potential Peltola win if votes for the second Sullivan could have changed the outcome, and a senior DOJ official told Fox News on Thursday that the criminal investigation has intensified, with officials examining possible civil-rights violations under 18 U.S.C. §§ 241 and 242. Vice President JD Vance said authorities should "certainly look into whether [Peltola] committed election fraud," describing the effort as an attempt to "steal a Senate seat." Senate Majority Leader John Thune called it a "coordinated effort" and "totally dirty pool." SEN DAN SULLIVAN BRANDS PELTOLA’S ALLEGED BALLOT SCHEME A ‘SCANDAL AT THE HIGHEST ORDER’ There is an "aggressive criminal investigation" into Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. appearing on the ballot, sources told Fox News. That investigation has only intensified since the Times' reporting but has been underway for several months. This investigation, being run by the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Alaska, is expected to go beyond Tuesday's Election Day, and there will not be any sort of indictment or heavy grand jury activity before then. 'DECOY DAN' SULLIVAN CASE LEADS TOP SENATOR TO BREAK FOUR-YEAR X SILENCE: 'PATTERN OF LIES' The DOJ thus far has declined to comment on the matter. Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy has also ordered a state investigation. Peltola’s campaign and DSCC officials have denied involvement in recruiting the second Sullivan to confuse voters, issuing warnings that "both sides" put up spoiler candidates in elections. The Alaska Supreme Court previously ruled the second Dan Sullivan could remain on the ballot under state law. "The RNC is heavily invested in protecting the vote in Alaska since this scheme came out," Triolo said. "We've been fighting it, drawing attention to it, doing everything we can to educate voters. DEM BUCKS PARTY OVER ALLEGED ALASKA VOTE-SIPHONING EFFORT: 'NEITHER PARTY SHOULD BE DOING IT' "We are heavily invested in securing Alaska and obviously this scheme is an absolute fraud. You saw President Trump come forward and say that Mary Peltola, the fake Dan Sullivan, all of these individuals should be held accountable not only for lying about their affiliation with the scheme, but also just for trying to deceive voters. "We are seeing this play out in real time. Even The New York Times, the left-wing media, has no choice but to hold them accountable for their schemes. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "So I think what we need to stay focused on, as Republicans, is that we need to keep the majority. This is why this midterm election feels like a presidential, because so much is at stake." Fox News' David Spunt, William Mears and Jake Gibson contributed to this report.

articles.title: As Trump escalates extreme attacks, Democrats – finally – rally round El-Sayed
articles.summary: Endorsement not always full-throated but party backing marks major turn after bitter split over nomination
articles.body:
Facing a barrage of extreme attacks from Donald Trump and his allies, the Democratic establishment is finally rallying around progressive Abdul El-Sayed, the party's candidate in the closely watched US Senate election in Michigan. But the endorsement is not always full-throated, and often even omits his name.

At a rally in Port Huron on Sunday, the US president launched the latest in a wave of Islamophobic rants against El-Sayed, erroneously branding him a "jihadist" and "Muslim Brotherhood member" while invoking 9/11.

But prominent Democrats have lined up to support El-Sayed. That same weekend, the independent senator Bernie Sanders rallied with him in Grand Rapids, and former president Barack Obama stood beside him in Detroit. Days earlier, the New York congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez toured the state with him.

This last-ditch show of solidarity marks a turn for a party that split bitterly over El-Sayed's nomination in August, which he narrowly clinched by beating a moderate pro-Israel candidate backed by much of the central party machine.

The Michigan Senate race – which could help decide which party controls the entire chamber – is close, according to polls, which have typically given El-Sayed a small lead over his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers.

Senior Democrats have increasingly traveled to Michigan to back a nominee who many of the party's leaders did not back in the primary – while making clear they are not fully aligned.

In an effort to close the gap, Republicans have doubled down on their incendiary attacks. Trump has repeatedly called him "Mohammed" this month, and the National Republican Senatorial Committee has aired ads using his full name, Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed.

El-Sayed, who was born in Michigan to Egyptian immigrants, has dismissed such attacks as a distraction. "He knows my name is Abdul. He says it every day," he said in a statement, accusing the president of trying to "use my name and my faith to distract us" from the cost of gas, groceries and healthcare.

A former Detroit and Wayne county health official, El-Sayed is running on a platform that endorses the Medicare for All proposed system of universal healthcare, and calls for taking corporate money out of politics, taxing billionaires and corporations and abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). He has also called for ending US military aid to Israel, while calling its war in Gaza a genocide.

A Marist poll last week put El-Sayed at 50% and Rogers at 48% among likely voters. He was trailing by nearly two to one in ad spending as of early October.

Obama's Saturday appearance in Detroit was the clearest sign of the shift by the Democrat party heirarchy. He joined El-Sayed on stage on the first day of early voting – his first public show of support for El-Sayed since the August primary – while a protest held by the white nationalist and 6 January rioter Jake Lang took place outside.

The former president likened the attacks on El-Sayed's name to those he faced himself. "I remind them his name was Barack," El-Sayed said.

Obama, whose 57% favorable rating in a CNN poll conducted in May is the highest of any living president, also rejected the idea that El-Sayed is radical. "What is so radical about wanting everybody to have healthcare?" he asked, saying El-Sayed would "finish the job we started" with the Affordable Care Act.

But Obama acknowledged that he did not agree with El-Sayed, who has criticized some of his decisions as president, all the time. "We are not going to agree on every detail of every issue," he said. "You know who else doesn't agree with everything I do? Michelle Obama."

Both Ocasio-Cortez and Sanders have transferred $1m to the El-Sayed campaign. Former vice-president Kamala Harris appeared with him in Detroit last month.

Senator Elissa Slotkin, who spoke at the same rally, told the crowd she was counting on El-Sayed as a partner in confronting Trump's agenda in Congress. Yet she has also said she and El-Sayed "don't agree on everything — and that's OK", and previously argued that condemning the leftwing streamer Hasan Piker, with whom El-Sayed has campaigned , should not be hard.

Others have been more guarded. The Senate Democratic leader,Chuck Schumer, who has now endorsed El-Sayed, said his views on Israel were "much different than mine", while the former congressman Sander Levin endorsed him despite what he called "significant disagreement" on the same subject. Representative Hillary Scholten said she would not campaign with anyone who associates with Piker.

Senator Cory Booker of New Jersey, who has historically been pro-Israel, gave a similarly noncommittal answer on CNN on Wednesday, when anchor Boris Sanchez played a clip of a Black pastor saying some voters fear that El-Sayed would prioritize issues abroad such as Gaza over Michigan's needs.

Booker spoke about his family roots in Michigan and about "winning back the Senate" without mentioning El-Sayed by name. When Sanchez pointed out to him this was not "a ringing endorsement", Booker remained stone-faced, and the segment continued.

But the coolest response came from Haley Stevens, the pro-Israel congresswoman El-Sayed beat in August by less than a point. She had been backed by groups including the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) , which spent close to $30m backing her – the lobby's largest investment in a single race.

Asked by CNN's Dana Bash on Sunday whether she was still fully behind him, she said she was "on the team". "You didn't mention Abdul El-Sayed in that last answer," Bash noted. Stevens replied that she had urged El-Sayed to give a speech addressing Black voters' concerns, and that it had not happened.

In the primary, Stevens beat El-Sayed in Wayne county, home to majority-Black Detroit, taking about 51% of the Democratic vote to his 45%. Obama urged Saturday's crowd to back the full ticket.

El-Sayed and Stevens are set to campaign together on Sunday – two days before election day – it emerged last night, in what would be their first joint public appearance in months.

Rogers, meanwhile, is courting Jewish voters, traditionally more likely to back Democrats, by telling the Jewish Telegraphic Agency that El-Sayed is "anti-Jew", a charge El-Sayed rejects.

Whether a cautious and caveated embrace by the Democratic establishment is enough for El-Sayed will be settled on Tuesday, in a state Trump won by less than two points in 2024.

If El-Sayed wins, he would be the first Muslim US senator. To get there, he has already pulled a skeptical party machine toward his side.

articles.title: Oleshky residents leave Russian-occupied city as evacuation corridor opens
articles.summary: Several hundred people are understood to have decided to stay in the frontline town, despite the lack of gas, electricity and running water.
articles.body:
The evacuation of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky is under way, Russian and Ukrainian authorities have confirmed.

A ceasefire, brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump, has been in force in the entire frontline region of Kherson since Tuesday, allowing for the road out of Oleshky to be demined.

Residents of Oleshky who wished to leave had a four-hour window to do so. A convoy of 25 buses was brought in to allow up to 750 people to leave the town until 14:00 (12:00 GMT), along with ambulances for people with limited mobility.

Several hundred people are understood to have decided to stay, despite the widespread devastation and the lack of gas, electricity and running water.

"Everyone who wishes to leave Oleshky will be given the opportunity to do so safely," Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said.

"At the same time, those who decide to remain will be able to stay and will receive all the necessary humanitarian assistance."

Ukrainian territory lies 5km (3.1miles) from Oleshky, but the evacuees will first have to travel into Russian-occupied territory and then to the southern Russian city of Anapa.

They will board a Russian government plane to Gomel in Belarus, and then drive across the border into Ukraine's Chernihiv region.

Others are expected to choose to stay in Russian-occupied territory.

Lubinets and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova travelled to Oleshky together on Friday, setting off from Armiansk, in the Russian-occupied Crimean peninsula.

Lubinets is the first Ukrainian official since the start of the war to visit Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine. He will also become the first to visit Russia when he escorts the evacuees back into Ukraine on Saturday.

The Oleshky ceasefire has required close cooperation with Lantratova, which Lubinets said he carried out in the interests of saving lives.

But some in Ukraine have recoiled at the sight of him standing beside a representative of the Russian occupying power which has killed so many of the city's residents and made life unbearable for the rest.

Both Lubinets and Lantratova posted videos from Oleshky on their social media channels, saying people were given the chance to form two groups depending on whether they wanted to be taken to Russian-controlled territory or to Ukraine.

In one video, Lubinets can be seen meeting tearful locals. "The problem is that a lot of people are staying," he can be heard saying. "I was told that it was their own choice, we will do everything possible for the humanitarian aid to arrive."

Russia said on Thursday that it had prepared "dozens of tonnes" of aid for the residents who do not wish to leave, including food, medicine, hygiene products and fuel for generators.

An Oleshky resident told the BBC she had decided against leaving because "they wouldn't take my animals, so that's it."

Olena, who now lives in Kyiv, said her grandmother and wider family in Oleshky were also staying behind.

"The older generation does not want to leave," she told the BBC. "I've barely managed to persuade my father - and only because I've just had a baby, who he would never see otherwise."

Olena's grandmother's sister died in Oleshky last winter.

"She lost her legs after stepping on a landmine, covered in snow... People took her to the hospital in a garden wheelbarrow," Olena said.

"That's how locals transport all wounded and dead people in Oleshky to the hospital and the hospital's morgue: in garden wheelbarrows."

The ceasefire is due to be in force until the end of Sunday 1 November. It has provided the first few days of peace in the Kherson region since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Residents of Kherson told the BBC they were "overjoyed" by the ceasefire. However, they are concerned the truce has given Russia time to build up its military presence on the banks of the Dnipro river, which could result in a renewed assault once the ceasefire expires.

On Friday, the Kremlin made it clear that the success of the Oleshky ceasefire should not be interpreted as willingness to extend the truce to the rest of Ukraine.

A handful of foreign journalists have been invited to witness the evacuation of the town, which Moscow is expected to present as a humanitarian mission conducted with mercy to protect the people of Oleshky.

Many Ukrainians suspect Russia's real intention is to earn credit with the White House, and to provide US President Donald Trump with a boost ahead of next week's midterm elections.

articles.title: Sen. Mark Kelly update: ‘anti-Trump’ 2028 presidential candidate or Senate reelection
articles.summary: Sen. Mark Kelly has emerged as a leading Democratic contender for the 2028 presidency following his recent involvement in a controversy regarding military obedience and his success in raising funds during the midterms.
articles.body:
The most contentious , expensive, dramatic, vitriolic , polarized, and gerrymandered midterm election in U.S. history peaks on Nov. 3, a campaign cycle in which President Trump repeatedly asked voters to “pretend” he was on the ballot.

Thus, Trump risks a personal rebuke if Democrats win control of the House and Senate and he deems the results of selected races fraudulent, rigged or stolen from Republicans. Such a scenario could trigger a constitutional crisis if the president authorizes aggressive federal action that Team Trump has loosely threatened throughout 2026.

Strangely, last Saturday, Trump sent an awkward fundraising email pleading, “Do not make me say goodbye.” Perhaps it was a smoke signal testing an early exit before Jan. 20, 2029? Furthermore, Trump officially becomes a “ lame duck ” on Nov. 4, the kick-off for the 2028 presidential campaign, which will make this nasty midterm election look like child’s play.

Although Vice President JD Vance has the edge for the Republican nomination, “when” or “if” Trump endorses him remains the wild card . Recently, on the campaign trail, Vance suffered a self-inflicted wound while defending a vile ad that could permanently haunt his standing with women voters.

Democrats have a deeper primary bench with no clear frontrunner. As a former Republican, my preferred candidate is Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.), who has 3 percent primary support. He is the anti-Trump candidate, opposite in personality and style for what is likely to be a pendulum-swing election. Kelly appears well suited for the post-Trump era, when America faces its most challenging domestic and foreign threats since the 1930s.

Exactly a year ago, my Hill op-ed , “Mark Kelly: former Space Shuttle commander to 2028 commander-in-chief?” drew eye rolls from political strategists. After discovering that was available, I bought it on a whim.

Fast forward to Kelly’s Oct. 20 interview on The Hill . It was reported that “He’s getting closer to making a decision about running for president.” But not until “the other side of this election,” Kelly explained. If yes, I will donate the domain to his campaign.

On Nov. 18, 2025, 11 days after my op-ed, Kelly appeared in a controversial video with five other lawmakers, urging military service members to defy illegal orders. As a result, Kelly is embroiled in several legal battles with the Trump administration and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The disputes have escalated and remain unresolved.

President Trump’s reaction to the video — exclaiming it was “seditious behavior, punishable by DEATH!” — propelled Kelly into the media spotlight, expanding his national profile and fundraising among Democrats.

A year later, Kelly is widely considered a prospective 2028 Democratic nominee. During the midterm election cycle, he raised over $14 million for candidates, developing a national network worthy of a presidential launch.

In the Senate, Kelly serves on the powerful Armed Services and Intelligence committees. He knows that accelerating technological change is significantly affecting the U.S. economy and, given its critical national security implications, must be harnessed to America’s advantage.

For Kelly, a space war is more than a presidential campaign talking point. Then, land wars in Europe and the Middle East, along with a potential Chinese invasion of Taiwan, call for someone with his background and experience to provide domestic and global leadership, given his heroic and inspiring resume.

Navy Capt. Kelly (retired) was a fighter and test pilot with 375 carrier landings and 39 combat missions. Later, as a NASA astronaut , he flew four Space Shuttle missions from 2001 to 2011, two as pilot and two as commander. His nerves of steel would serve him well during an intense primary, an off-the-charts general election, and in the Oval Office.

Tragically, astronaut Kelly’s life changed in January 2011, when his wife, then-Rep. Gabby Giffords (D-Ariz.), was shot in the head at a mass-casualty event. To support her long recovery, Kelly retired from NASA. Today, Giffords advocates against gun violence despite a speech disability caused by brain damage. They are a team should Kelly run for president.

However, they must decide between a crowded, brutal Democratic primary and a Senate reelection campaign. In 2022, Kelly won with only 51 percent, although politically stronger now. He could choose the Senate and possibly be tapped as the nominee’s running mate. In 2024, Kamala Harris considered Kelly for her vice president but chose the governor of Minnesota instead.

If Kelly enters the primary, he will lose the hair war to the photogenic California Gov. Gavin Newsom if Newsom runs. But central-casting looks shouldn’t matter when Kelly’s unique skill set and experience can help the U.S. regain respect among our allies and trading partners, boosting the American economy after years of Trump’s alienating policies.

In a world increasingly dominated by high-tech weaponized threats, an aeronautical engineer, space shuttle commander, and battleground-state senator might swing the political pendulum away from Trump’s reign of error. Mark Kelly retired to care for his wife, demonstrating he is empathetic, emotionally stable, authentic, and eminently qualified to be the next commander in chief. Call him the “anti-Trump.”

Myra Adams served on the creative team of two Republican presidential campaigns in 2004 and 2008. Read more from her archive at The Hill .

articles.title: Five of the most expensive races this cycle
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Following the midterm money ▪ Final economic reports before Election Day ▪ Trump cancels Iowa, Kansas rallies ▪ Elon Musk in the crosshairs The 2026 midterms have officially become the most expensive election cycle ever, with a handful of races dominating the ad spending charts. On Monday, the current cycle reached…
articles.body:
▪ Final economic reports before Election Day

The 2026 midterms have officially become the most expensive election cycle ever, with a handful of races dominating the ad spending charts.

On Monday, the current cycle reached $11.21 billion in ad spending and reservations, surpassing the $11.2 billion spent during the 2024 cycle, which included $3.2 billion for just the presidential race, according to AdImpact .

The firm also found that four races this year rank among the 10 most expensive nonpresidential races on record, with a fifth race this cycle not far behind. The totals below account for ad spending and future reservations through Oct. 27 and include spending in both primary and general elections.

Here are five of the most expensive races this cycle:

The U.S. Senate race in Texas has become the single most expensive nonpresidential race of all time, with $557.6 million in ad spending and future reservations as of Tuesday.

That number includes the notoriously expensive primaries earlier this year. In the general election match-up between Democratic nominee James Talarico and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, Republicans have spent more than double what Democrats have spent on the race, according to a separate AdImpact general-election update released yesterday.

Republicans have spent $269.4 million on the general election alone, while Democrats have spent $130.8 million.

However, Talarico has raised more direct donations, while Paxton has largely relied on PAC money, meaning the Democrat is getting a lot more bang for his buck down the home stretch.

The Ohio special Senate race crossed $500 million in ad spending and reservations this week, making this cycle the only one on record to have multiple races surpass half a billion dollars.

This year’s Senate race in Ohio ranks as the third most expensive nonpresidential race of all time, falling behind the 2024 Ohio Senate race, when former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio) was unseated by Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio).

The state got two new senators that following January, when Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) was appointed to fill the seat vacated by Vice President Vance . Brown is now trying to earn his seat back, as Husted, the former lieutenant governor, seeks to win his first election for his Senate seat.

California’s governor’s race has drawn $349.4 million in ad spending and reservations as of Tuesday, becoming the most expensive governor’s race ever, though much of that money was spent on the crowded primary race.

By the June primary, spending had already reached $315.8 million, with billionaire Democrat Tom Steyer accounting for $201.2 million of that total before he lost.

In the general election, former Health and Human Services Secretary Xavier Becerra (D) is heavily favored to defeat former Fox News host Steve Hilton (R).

According to AdImpact’s Tuesday ranking, the 2026 governor’s race ranks seventh on the list of all-time most expensive nonpresidential races.

In eighth place on the all-time list, as of Tuesday, Michigan’s open Senate race had drawn $347.5 million in ad spending and reservations, as Democrat Abdul El-Sayed faces off against former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) for retiring Sen. Gary Peters ‘s (D-Mich.) seat.

The primaries alone saw $98.2 million by July 31, a few days before the election, already more than tripling the state’s previous record for a nonpresidential primary. That made it the third most expensive Senate primary on record, according to AdImpact, behind this year’s Senate race in Texas and the 2022 Senate race in Arizona. Much of that spending went to El-Sayed’s Democratic opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.).

A separate AdImpact update released yesterday put Republican general election spending in Michigan at $143.5 million, compared with Democrats’ $117 million.

The state’s 2020 special election for Senate ranked 10th in AdImpact’s tally, with $303.5 million spent on that race. But this year’s contest for governor falls not far behind, with $297 million spent as of Monday on aired ads and future reservations. That total is largely driven by the $268.5 million in GOP spending — mostly from the personal fortune of Republican nominee Rick Jackson.

Much of the total spending was dished out during the primaries. By mid-June, just days before the GOP runoff, the race had already drawn more than $162 million in advertising, according to AdImpact data analyzed by the Wesleyan Media Project. Republican candidates accounted for roughly $133.6 million of that.

Jackson, a healthcare executive, now faces former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms (D) in the race to succeed term-limited Gov. Brian Kemp (R). Polling shows the race in a statistical dead heat.

▪ The Hill : Senate Democrats’ PAC spends in South Carolina for first time.

▪ The Hill : Lingering Democratic divisions could preview 2028 challenges.

Federal and state investigations are underway in Alaska involving allegations that Democrats tried to stack the ballot with someone who has the same name as the Republican Senate candidate. According to our parters at Decision Desk HQ, Democratic candidate Mary Peltola has a 60 percent chance to defeat Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska). I asked Gov. Mike Dunleavy (R) if his state would certify the election if Peltola wins and the investigation is still ongoing.

“We’re going to investigate. If we find out there’s wrongdoing, and if that means that the certification then is stopped or changed, then that’s what happens. But we’re going to work through this thing methodically so that everyone believes that this is done the right way,” Dunleavy said.

According to DDHQ, there’s a 12 percent chance the result in Alaska ends up determining who will control the Senate. However, there appears to be a possibility that Election Day might not be the finish line for the race in Alaska.

By the way, we are having our last Viewer’s Voice segment before the midterms. Want your questions answered by Congress? Email me and my team at viewersvoice@newsnationnow.com . We will put them before Rep. Henry Cuellar (D-Texas) later tonight.

Burman hosts “The Hill” weeknights, 6 p.m. EDT/5 p.m. CDT on NewsNation.

The controversial ad from Ohio GOP gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy featuring Amy Acton’s estranged mother is no longer airing , as the campaign said it ran its course. The ad stirred significant backlash to Ramaswamy from both Republicans and Democrats.

DoorDash plans to acquire Instacart for about $17 billion, making it one of the largest grocery delivery companies in the U.S. if it is approved. Instacart will keep its brand name , and customers will be able to continue using the app for their grocery shopping orders.

The head of a Vietnam veterans group told The Washington Post he was misled before the organization endorsed President Trump’s planned 250-foot triumphal arch. A federal judge will hear arguments today on whether to allow construction on the arch to proceed.

Cash is fanned out from a wallet in North Andover, Mass, June 15, 2018. (Elise Amendola, Associated Press file)

FINAL COUNT : The final economic indicators ahead of the midterms were revealed Thursday as the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) showed economic growth and inflation both ticked up.

The country’s gross domestic product increased at an annual rate of 3.4 percent during the third quarter of 2026, from July through September. That’s a jump from the 2.2 percent increase from the second quarter and 2.5 percent from the first.

The boost came as investment in artificial intelligence has surged, with Big Tech companies racing to build out data centers all over the country.

“The U.S. economy is on steroids right now. Growth came in stronger than expected and it’s largely due to the massive AI business investment surge,” Heather Long , the chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, wrote to The Hill.

But the strong economic growth came with more inflation. BEA showed the personal consumption expenditures price index, the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation metric, rose by 0.5 percent last month. It was up 3.6 percent relative to September 2025.

That’s well above the Fed’s 2 percent target for inflation. The agency voted to keep interest rates steady at its meeting Wednesday but is expected to raise rates in December.

▪ CNBC : How affordability, the economy could affect voters’ decisions.

▪ Axios : Long-term care enters affordability debate.

STRICT SCRUTINY : House Oversight Committee Chair James Comer (R-Ky.) launched an investigation Thursday into Mary Peltola ‘s campaign following a New York Times report that it sought to recruit candidates to take votes away from incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska).

“Americans deserve answers about this latest attempt by Democrats to defraud the American people, and we will get them,” Comer said in a statement.

He sent letters to Peltola’s former campaign manager and a Democratic operative whom the Times reported was also involved in the alleged operation, requesting they sit for in-person transcribed interviews.

The announcement came after Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy (R) ordered an investigation into whether Peltola’s campaign violated state law.

Ballot “stacking” is a practice that has been used by both parties and is not considered to be illegal. Peltola’s campaign had denied any involvement in recruiting another candidate named Dan J. Sullivan .

▪ The Hill : Republicans have knives out for Peltola.

▪ The Associated Press : Justice Department issues new subpoenas in probe.

VIRTUAL SHIFT : The president is wrapping up his midterm campaign blitz with mostly virtual appearances after traveling all around the country this week.

Trumpwas scheduled to travel to Kansas on Saturday to campaign for Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) and Iowa on Sunday, but a White House official confirmed to The Hill that the in-person events had been cancelled .

“The demand for POTUS [president of the United States] to hold rallies has been huge from our candidates, and we are adjusting to a tele-rally to maximize his reach and communicate with as many voters as possible,” a GOP source said.

The announcement comes as Marshall is fighting for his political life in a close contest against Democrat Adam Hamilton .

Trump is expected to hold telerallies across 19 states in the coming days. He is still scheduled to travel to Daytona Beach, Fla., tonight to campaign for Florida’s Republican candidates.

▪ The Hill : Trump hammers culture war attacks in final South Carolina rally.

▪ The Hill : Vance makes fiery closing pitch for Ken Paxton.

The president will participate in a radio interview at 7:30 a.m. and a pre-taped interview at 1:30 p.m. He will travel to Daytona Beach, Fla., and participate in a telerally on the way at 5 p.m. He will then deliver remarks in Daytona Beach at 7 p.m. before traveling to Palm Beach.

Elon Musk listens as President Donald Trump speaks during an event at the U.S. Institute of Peace, Oct. 8, 2026, in Washington. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson, Associated Press)

SPOTLIGHT EFFECT : The controversy surrounding Ukraine’s access to Starlink and its military version Starshield is casting an spotlight on Elon Musk ‘s enormous influence on the world stage.

Musk acknowledged after about 10 days of confusion and finger-pointing that his company, SpaceX, was responsible for the slowdown of Ukraine’s connectivity.

The Hill’s Julia Shapero and Miranda Nazarro report that who exactly made the decision to slow Starshield down remains contested, but the chaos is underscoring the reach that Musk has on global and military affairs.

“A lot of people are uncomfortable with the idea that an individual like a corporate leader, [is] essentially making foreign policy decisions about access, though it’s not clear what the alternative is in this case,” Michael Horowitz , director of the Defense and National Security program at the Council on Foreign Relations, told The Hill.

Ukraine has relied on Starlink’s commercial services since the Russia-Ukraine war began in 2022. The country later added Starshield through SpaceX’s contract with the Pentagon.

Musk argued Saturday that using the commercial service for “offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be.” Ukrainian officials disputed that it violated the terms of service.

The incident raised concerns among members of both parties about the U.S. being overly reliant on Musk.

▪ The Hill : Backlash to AI data centers threatens GOP’s grip on Ohio, Texas.

Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney, front left, speaks with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, eastern France, Sept 17, 2026. (Pascal Bastien, Associated Press)

CLOSER BONDS : European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen continued her push to make Canada an “associate member” of the bloc during a meeting with Prime Minister Mark Carney in Montreal on Thursday.

E.U. members including France and Germany have reportedly pushed back on the designation, while still supporting a closer relationship with Canada. However, von der Leyen isn’t giving up on the proposal, which she first floated earlier this year.

She said Canada and the EU would form the core of the proposed “Alliance for the Future ” and other like-minded countries are welcome to join, boosting collective resiliency around critical minerals, supply chains and security, The Associated Press reported .

Carney said the alliance would help Canada withstand economic shocks and limit influence from other countries and technology companies.

“Why does sovereignty matter in a dangerous and divided world? It allows us to withstand shocks,” Carney said at a news conference. “It allows us to live our lives as we choose.”

Carney and von der Leyen first raised the idea of Canada becoming an associate member last month following rising tension between Carney and Trump. The U.S. and Canada have been engaged in a trade war for weeks, slapping wide-ranging tariffs on a variety of goods.

“Canada cannot become a full-fledged member of the EU because of geography, but we both want to bring our relationship to the highest level possible,” von der Leyen said.

The race for Texas governor will decide control of the House , Rep. Linda Sánchez (D-Calif.) writes in The Hill.

To prevent the next Cornell 7 case, we must raise better men , Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) writes in The Hill.

People gather outside a hotel near a mural of Dolores Huerta during a vigil to honor the labor organizer, whose advocacy improved conditions for migrant farm workers, Oct. 28, 2026, in Los Angeles. (Jae C. Hong, Associated Press)

And finally … 👏👏👏 Congrats to this week’s Morning Report quiz winners ! Rest in peace, Dolores Huerta.

Here’s who went 4/4: Michael Salanik, Gail White, Harry Strulovici, Joe Winters, Rick Schmidtke, Jenessa Wagner, Jay Rockey, Julie Barnes, Linda L. Field, Wiley H. Pearson, David Newton, Carmine Petracca, JA Ramos, Daniel Beierman and Steve James .

Before she was a full-time organizer, Huerta worked as a schoolteacher .

Former President Obama credited Huerta with inspiring his campaign slogan, “Yes we can.” Huerta coined the rallying cry “Si, se puede!”

Huerta was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2012 by Obama.

New Mexico celebrates Dolores Huerta Day annually, since Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham (D) signed a bill establishing it into law in 2023. Lawmakers in Nevada passed a bill to establish the day last year, but Gov. Joe Lombardo (R) vetoed it .

articles.title: What Orson Welles’s ‘War of the Worlds’ broadcast tells us, 88 years later
articles.summary: Our current obsession with fake news really began 88 years ago.
articles.body:
On October 30, 1938, a broadcast interrupted dinners across America. This was the era of breaking news bulletins, and many thought it was the beginning of World War II.

Hitler had been threatening to invade Czechoslovakia to take back the Sudetenland. War had seemed imminent all through the month. But this was something different. Up in the radio studio at CBS in Manhattan a young man with a baritone voice was holding up his hands for six seconds of silence after a reporter had been burned alive on the radio. The boy wonder, Orson Welles, held the world in thrall with his Martians landing all over America and people running for the hills.

Halloween is upon us, and so is the 88th anniversary of Orson Welles’ broadcast of H.G. Wells’s “The War of the Worlds.” What started as the seventeenth program of Mercury Theatre on the Air quickly devolved into a terrifying news broadcast that Martians had landed in Grovers Mill, N.J. and emerged with heat ray guns and poisonous gas to exterminate humanity.

The Martians then headed for New York, and people headed for the countryside. They hid in basements and cars. They ran out of apartment buildings. They dashed from restaurants without paying. They ran into churches, out movie theatres, out of hospitals, weddings, schools, colleges — anything to get away from the advancing Martian’s that had suddenly had crossed the continental U.S., incinerated the army and were finishing off human life.

All this from the mind of a twenty-three-year-old on a brisk October night before Halloween. It was ingenious really. Take a science fiction novel by an English writer and turn it into a one hour drama with a breaking news format. Incinerate a reporter on the air and then go to six seconds of radio silence, or “dead air.”

This is where Welles shined. He turned this moment of silence into a moment of terror and made the radio a character, breaking the fourth wall. We are used to that now, with characters talking to the camera in everything from “The Big Short” to “The Office.” But in 1938, no one came out from behind the curtain.

Welles did two things at once. He used the new medium of radio against itself by proclaiming a crisis, then had radio run away in panic as well. Brilliant. It was the first Fake News broadcast.

The blowback from this moment would change radio forever. Welles himself was headed for jail — or at least banishment or physical harm with death threats and lawsuits raining down on CBS and himself. CBS held a famous news conference, with him standing at the center, looking like the title character of “ Peck’s Bad Boy ” pleading innocence.

It didn’t work, but then Dorothy Thompson the leading columnist of her day turned the pandemonium on its head and told the world Orson had done everyone a favor by showing how ignorant, how uneducated, how gullible the American public was. It was a warning to wake up, or else Hitler and Mussolini would soon be marching down Fifth Avenue.

Just like that, Welles was proclaimed a genius and headed to Hollywood to make his opus, “Citizen Kane.”

Orson later admitted to his prank on the BBC. He claimed he did it because people believed just about anything coming through the radio. He wanted to show we should question what we heard.

The thought that a 23-year-old could cause coast-to-coast panic today with a broadcast about invading Martians does seem absurd to our Twenty-First Century sensibilities. People have said this type of panic could never happen again. But when my book came out a few years back on the broadcast , “ Dead Air: The Night Orson Welles Terrified America ,” there were drones in the skies over America. President Joe Biden was telling us not to worry, but social media lit up with aliens and Martians invading.

Our current obsession with fake news really began 88 years ago, when Welles grabbed our anxiety and took it out for a night ride.

William Elliott Hazelgrove is the author of “Dead Air: The Night Orson Welles Terrified America.”

articles.title: Live updates: Trump to campaign for GOP candidates in Florida
articles.summary: Live updates and the latest news as Trump rallies for GOP candidates in Florida and James Comey’s lawyers head to court seeking to have a federal criminal case against him tossed out.
articles.body:
What to know today TRUMP HEADS TO FLORIDA: President Donald Trump will hold a rally in Daytona Beach tonight to campaign for Republican candidates, including Rep. Bryon Donalds, Sen. Ashely Moody and Rep. Randy fine, the nominees for governor, Senate and House, respectively. articles.body:
Watch Whole Hog Politics Live : Hill Insider members can join us live today at 9 a.m. EDT as Chris Stirewalt and host Bill Sammon go deep on this week’s political news. Members can join the discussion and pose their questions to Bill and Chris. Tune in!

The general premise of this note is that normal people want to follow politics, too. OK, maybe “need” is a better word, since wanting to follow politics closely these days would be a sure marker of abnormality.

There are a lot of places where you can go to get a constant transfusion of all the contradictory conjecture, spin, scooplet and data drops that your heart desires. But why do that, when you can pay us to do it for you? We comb through the minutiae and then, taking a longer, broader view, offer you a primer in the hope that we can discard some debris and, with respect for your time and attention, give you a weekly rundown of what’s happening.

This is our last note before the end of a midterm election cycle that began in earnest last spring when Texas kicked off a gerrymandering war, then intensified with off-year contests in Virginia and New Jersey, and then roared into a wild-and-wooly primary season in early 2026.

We’ve been offering you polling averages on President Trump ’s job approval rating and national voters’ preferences for partisan control of Congress. In our final, preelection tabulation we find the president at 34.6 percent, down 6 points from a year ago, and the preference for Democratic control at 52 percent, up 4.8 points from a year ago.

For some basic framing, just imagine that someone told you a year ago that those numbers would have moved in those directions by those amounts. Given the GOP bloodbath that was taking place in Virginia and New Jersey, you’d figure that the midterms would be pretty rough for Republicans. And you would have been right.

For a lot of reasons relating to the gaming of expectations, intraparty positioning, looming presidential nomination contests and the political media’s tendency to build and then break narratives, it feels like the midterm climate has been full of wild swings. But if you skipped the previous 11 months and tuned in for the season finale, you would have missed some truly wild story arcs and crazy characters, but you would certainly know the plot.

Elections are wonderful things. There’s the pageant of democracy and the power of the people to fire their leaders. But there’s also the beautiful quality of their ending . We’ve lived in a world of “the permanent campaign” for decades, but the conclusion of elections, thank God, offers a pause. The people have spoken and everybody has to like it or lump it. The next cycle begins almost at once, but the reality benders of politics and media are, for a time at least, obliged to reset their spin cycles.

How well or poorly you think the parties do next week will mostly depend on your own allegiances. Democrats will be disappointed if they don’t score upsets in several deep-red states, and Republicans will be cheered if they manage to hang on in some places that the president won by more than a dozen points two years ago. Partisanship, it is rightly said, is a hell of a drug.

Now, we want you to stay up all night, glued to your television watching special coverage from NewsNation and the latest race calls from our partners at Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). While you’re at it, keep refreshing The Hill, clicking with wild abandon on the latest returns. You could rewatch old Whole Hog Politics videos on YouTube on a third screen. And as you stare, bleary-eyed at me, even blearier-eyed, at 2 a.m. EST as we wait for inklings from Alaska’s Mat-Su Valley you can feel that you are truly one with the great demos of the United States.

Or, maybe you have a job. Perhaps you have children who would like breakfast at 7 o’clock in the morning, regardless of how gripping you found the mail-in ballots from Idaho. We’ve got you covered.

We’re going to know a great deal about how the election went by 8 p.m., and by 10 p.m., it’s probably going to be all over but the shouting. We know this for a couple of reasons. First, how the votes are counted doesn’t have anything to do with how they are cast. About half of all ballots will have been submitted prior to Election Day. By that evening, as the polls are starting to close, we will be down to just a handful of stragglers. When you’re watching election coverage, you’re watching an unboxing of a completed product, not the creation of something new.

Second, similar voters tend to vote similarly. We are a wildly diverse continental republic that comprises a dizzying array of cultures and characters. But, with a profoundly nationalized form of politics these days, demographically similar voters in one part of the country tend to behave in similar ways, i.e., married white women with college degrees in Georgia may tend to be more Republican than their counterparts in Washington state, but history tells us that they will swing in similar directions by similar amounts.

Indeed, the country as a whole tends to swing one way or another. There will be some exceptions, and different regions will move more than others, but there will be a theme to the pudding next week. And, luckily, we will get a good taste of what’s happening even before primetime begins as states on the East Coast and in the Midwest start reporting their returns.

How much we will be able to say about the final disposition of the fight for the Senate and the House will depend on how big the swing is. If it’s a bigger blue wave than expected or if Republicans have rallied and rebuilt their red wall, we will be able to draw a lot of conclusions by, say, 8:30 p.m. Conversely, if the polling has been reliable and many of these races really are very close, we’re going to have to wait at least another hour before we get a sense of where the sea of ballots is going to crest.

With that in mind, we’re offering you the Whole Hog Politics guide to the first half of election night, or, if you like, how to sound like a pro to your family and friends even if you actually have a life.

After the jump, we’re going to lay out the poll closings in Eastern Standard Time from 6 p.m. until 9 p.m. We’ll offer you a guide to key races and, crucially, key counties that will tell us how voters are moving. While others are fuming at a graphic that is stuck at “72 percent of expected votes counted,” you’ll be able to zoom in on bellwether counties to see what’s likely to happen in the states and races as a whole.

So, save this email, and, on Tuesday, when you fire up the flatscreen and pass the pork rinds, you’ll be ahead of the game. And when your eyelids get heavy, you can go to bed with a pretty good idea of what you’ll be waking up to, other than a request for sliced bananas in the oatmeal.

Thanks for riding along with us this cycle. We’ll be back next week to tell you what we actually learned from voters and what it means going forward. Happy viewing!

Programming alert: Watch a special, preelection double dose of “The Hill Sunday” with Chris Stirewalt — Catch us at 10 a.m. EST on NewsNation or check your local listings to find the affiliate in your area. Then, stick around for a second hour on NewsNation as we dive deeper into the trends and stories shaping the midterm vote. We’ll have live reports from battleground states, and guests include Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin , former Republican National Committee Chair Ronna McDaniel , Jessica Taylor of the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter , Sean Trende of RealClearPolitics, Scott Tranter of Decision Desk HQ, Chuck Lane of the Free Press, and Margaret Talev of Syracuse University.

Holy croakano! We welcome your feedback, so please email us with your tips, corrections, reactions, amplifications, etc. at WholeHogPolitics@TheHill.com . articles.title: Angie Nixon’s ignorance on Cuba shows she isn’t ready for the Senate
articles.summary: Mike Waltz needs to school Angie Nixon about Cuba. When CBS News reporter Cristian Benavides asked…
articles.body:
Mike Waltz needs to school Angie Nixon about Cuba.

Nixon, a Democrat aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America who is running to become a U.S. senator from Florida, recently showed extreme and perhaps willful ignorance about the communist country perched just 90 miles off her state’s coast.

When CBS News reporter Cristian Benavides asked Nixon if she considers Cuba a dictatorship, she responded, “That is what people have told me. I have never been to Cuba, and so I will have to take their word for it.”

Coming from someone running for statewide office in Florida, home to more than a million Cuban exiles and their families, Nixon’s tone-deaf response was rebuked not only by Republicans but also by other Democratic candidates in the Sunshine State.

Does she not actually know the miserable history of Cuba’s repressive and brutal communist regime? Nixon certainly could have benefitted from being in the room recently when Mike Waltz, the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, stunned the General Assembly by documenting the corruption and hardship delivered to the people of Cuba over the last 67 years.

Waltz addressed the Turtle Bay diplomats on the eve of their annual vote condemning the U.S. sanctions imposed on our southern neighbor, trying to interrupt a 34-year run of anti-American posturing. As he showed photos of Fidel Castro wearing not one but two Rolex watches at a time when Cubans could not afford basic necessities, Waltz declared, “According to the regime’s own statistics, that would pay for 55 years of an average Cuban wage.” Waltz also shared a photo of Cuba’s current ruler, Miguel Díaz-Canel. “It didn’t just start with Castro,” he said. “This is the current Cuban president, also with a Rolex on.”

Waltz also displayed pictures of the Castro family’s 14,000-square-foot seaside retreat and revealed that Cuba’s military-run conglomerate GAESA has stockpiled some $18 billion in looted funds. As reported by the New York Post, “Waltz called out the Havana government for profiting off of the forced labor of its own citizens sent to concentration camps while using confiscated ‘businesses, farms, factories, homes and the savings of generations of hardworking Cubans’ to line the pockets of its leaders.”

In response, Cuba’s delegates rushed the stage, attempting, as Waltz noted, to intimidate him. “I know that you don’t like to hear these hard truths, but I am speaking for the Cuban people,” Waltz said. “And ever since 1959, this government in Havana would have you believe that everything in Cuba has just disappeared; that they are the victim; that it’s someone else’s fault.”

Waltz is correct. Cuba and its few friends around the globe lay the country’s poverty and dysfunction at the feet of U.S. sanctions, first imposed by President Dwight Eisenhower in 1960 and now escalated under President Trump .

Most economists say it is the socialist policies embraced by the rulers of Cuba, not sanctions or John F. Kennedy’s 1962 embargo, that have caused its problems.

Why should we care? Because young people in our country appear enamored of socialism. It is important for them to know just what sort of misery has been delivered to humanity by what New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani calls the “warmth of collectivism” — in Cuba and elsewhere. Our schools have not educated our youth about the undeniable failures of communist and socialist nations, or about the successes of capitalism.

It is impossible to find a socialist country that has succeeded in improving the lives of its people. In 1970, Venezuela was the richest country in Latin America; today, after more than two decades of socialist rule, it is the poster child for socialism run amok. An economy in free fall, a bureaucracy riddled with rampant corruption and more than 70 percent of the people living in poverty — that is the sorry heritage of Hugo Chávez, who became president in 1998 . Chavez nationalized the oil industry and adopted leftist policies such as price controls and property expropriations. Venezuela descended into poverty. His successor, Nicolas Maduro, presided over a more than 75 percent shrinkage in his nation’s economy between 2014 and 2021.

Meanwhile, Venezuela became one of the most corrupt countries on earth , ranking ahead of only Sudan and Somalia on Transparency International’s 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index.

Cuba has followed the communist playbook since Fidel Castro took over in 1959. Before the revolution, Cuba’s GDP per capita ranked seventh among 47 Latin American economies. Soon after Castro took control, he nationalized key industries. By the late 1960s, Cuba was a ward of the Soviet Union, dependent on its communist overlords for economic, political and military aid.

The collapse of the Soviet Union caused a further decline in Cuba’s fortunes. GDP fell by 33 percent between 1990 and 1993 . The country was plagued by severe shortages of food, fuel and medicine.

After 50 years of communism, in 2001, Cuba was the third poorest country in Latin America as measured by per capita GDP. Only Nicaragua and desperately poor Haiti ranked lower.

The upshot has been a severe drop in population . According to the Council on Foreign Relations, “up to a quarter of the population has left since 2020.” Cuba’s repressive government, bent on locking up protesters, and the lack of opportunity in the communist country are together driving young people especially to escape. The council reports that more than 700 were arrested in the summer demonstrations against the regime’s repression.

Human Rights Watch reports that Cuba’s government “continues to repress and punish virtually all forms of dissent and public criticism”; they control all media and stage sham elections in which candidates are nominated by the government. Citizens can vote, but have no choice.

This is the country that Nixon could not bring herself to describe as a dictatorship. She is not ready to be a senator.

L iz Peek is a former partner of major bracket Wall Street firm Wertheim and Company.

articles.summary: Segunda comparecencia del ministro de Transportes tras el accidente ferroviario
articles.body: El ministro de Transportes, Óscar Puente, ha comparecido de nuevo, 48 horas después, para seguir aportando información al respecto de la investigación del accidente ferroviario de Urda, en Toledo. La tensión se deja notar a medida que van pasando las horas. Por todo ello, el Partido Popular ha pedido su dimisión por la crisis en sistema ferroviario español. Y el propio presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, ha admitido hoy mismo, tras la reunión del CECOPI, que "no son asumibles" dos accidentes ferroviarios sufridos en el último año que han dejado más de un centenar de víctimas mortales. Dicha comparecencia ha arrancado a las 12:00 horas donde ha señalado de primeras que está para explicar con rigor y proporcionalidad. No va a dimitir. "Respeto todas las opiniones pero la decisión no debe obedecer a la presión del momento". Ha incidido en que no va a "esconderse" detrás de ningún trabajador. Puente ha tenido unas palabras para los sindicatos ferroviarios y la oposición, que le acusan de cargar las tintas sobre el error de un trabajador, la teoría del "fallo humano", en vez de asumir su responsabilidad en el accidente de tren. "Si hubo fallos en los controles o la organización y si hubo responsabilidades individuales, se exigirán por los cauces correspondientes". Puente ha explicado de forma cronológica los hechos que ha ido detallando. "Equipos informáticos cuando cayó el LZTB los trenes se pararon, se opera desde Adif -bajo el BSL y el Asfa-...". ¿Por qué sucede el LZTB falle y ocurra?: "No sabemos qué generó el problema de comunicación. Hay que esperar que la empresa tenga el permiso correspondiente para analizarlo. Noes una incidencia infrecuente, pero el sistema de actuación está pautado en el reglamento que hay". Asegura que se han producido 160 incidencias en el sistema, pero ha defendido que es una media normal. "El LZTB lo tiene el 80% de la red alemana y austriaca, en líneas regionales de Reino Unido...". ¿Por qué se cambia? "Por motivos interoperabilidad y otro industrial... España es el país que ha implementado más kilómetros de RTMS en toda la Unión Europea. Es la primera que implementarlo. ¿Por qué no se ha hecho el cambio de sistemas? Estaba fijado para abril de 2026. "Esta implementación físicamente, concluyó en junio de 2026". ¿Cómo funciona el centro de Adif? "Control normal. Había 16 personas. Ha habido un incremento de plantilla de un 60% más las mejoras tecnológicas hechas. Nuestro trabajo ha sido incrementar la plantilla en España" El ministro ha mirado al centro de control de Adif si bien no ha querido señalar a nadie y lo ha vuelto a reiterar. "Yo no he hablado de error humano. He hablado de hechos. Sí hacer una auditoría y se pueden sacar ya conclusiones con el fin de recuperar la confianza". Ante la posibilidad de detener el servicio para remodelar: "Estamos valorando parar el tráfico. No sólo por cuestiones de seguridad". Cómo ha podido pasar: "No lo sabemos. Es incomprensible". "Es inasumible que haya dos accidente en menos de un año. Debemos garantizar y hacer cambios. Si se relaciona por una posible dimisión, soy muy pequeño para el proyecto de reforma.
