articles.title: Georgia midterm elections: Why this is a key US battleground
articles.summary: Obama and Trump campaign in key battleground state ahead of next week’s midterm elections.
articles.body:
Georgia is among a number of key “swing” or “battleground” states being fought for hardest in the run-up to the United States midterm elections next week.

The southern state has been so competitive in recent federal election cycles that its three most recent Senate matchups went to runoffs.

Both the Republican and the Democratic parties have spent considerable time and resources trying to win the state during the closing stretch of their campaigns.

US President Donald Trump and former US President Barack Obama both held rallies in Georgia this week, as the parties present their closing messages ahead of next week’s vote.

Why is Georgia such a key state for the midterms?

Georgia is a major focus for Trump, and he has campaigned twice in Dalton, Georgia, in the past two weeks.

The state is a source of personal grievance for the president, primarily because it was where he disputed his preelection loss in 2020.

Trump refused to concede to Joe Biden following his defeat but failed to overturn the results in several states, including Georgia.

In January, Trump urged a Georgia official to recalculate the state’s presidential election results in his favour. Trump said “I just want to find 11,780 votes, which is one more than we have”.

In 2023, Trump and others were charged with attempting to overturn the 2020 US election loss in Georgia. That case was dismissed “in its entirety” after Trump was returned to office.

During his re-election campaign in 2024, Trump revived unfounded claims that his loss in 2020 was the result of “massive fraud”, despite audits which upheld Biden’s win.

In 2024, Georgia voted for Trump by a 2.2 percentage point margin. It was the 28th largest margin for Trump among the 50 states, leaving the state as one which could go either way this time, observers say.

Georgia will be voting for its Governor, one senator and its House representatives.

For the Senate, incumbent Democrat Jon Ossoff has a solid lead of 52.6 percent to Republican Mike Collins’ 42.4 percent, according to MS NOW polling averages.

Polls indicate a tight Governor’s race, however. Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms is up against Republican Rick Jackson. They are running to succeed Republican Brian Kemp, who cannot seek a third term.

Voters will also be choosing representatives for Georgia’s 14 congressional districts as well as Lieutenant Governor, Attorney General and Secretary of State. Of the 14 representatives Georgia sends to Congress, nine are currently Republican, while five are Democratic.

Who are the key contenders for the Senate?

Incumbent Ossoff is seeking a second term as a Georgia senator. He won his seat in 2021, narrowly defeating Republican Senator David Perdue in a run-off. He was the youngest Democrat elected to the Senate in almost four decades and Georgia’s first Jewish senator.

He is campaigning on affordability, healthcare and government accountability.

Ossoff has accused Trump and his allies of corruption and conflicts of interest in many of his rallies.

Corruption was also a theme for Obama during his rally in Georgia on Wednesday, in which he said Trump was “very much focused on enriching himself and his family and his cronies”.

“The guy has made billions of dollars while in office. We have never seen a president so intent on selling favours like this,” he said, echoing a speech he made days earlier in Michigan, another swing state.

Ossoff’s Republican rival won his nomination in June in a run-off. Collins is campaigning on Trump’s agenda, immigration enforcement and smaller government.

During his last-minute rallies ahead of next week’s midterms, Trump has repeatedly said he will reward states that vote for him.

Trump told Collins he can call him whenever he wants help for his state. But he warned that if Georgia reelects Ossoff, it could be another story.

Trump acted out a hypothetical scenario at his rally where Ossoff called to ask for money for his state, with Trump responding, “I don’t give a damn what he wants.”

NBC, which carries out its own polling, has forecast Georgia as “Likely Democratic”.

Who are the key contenders for governor?

NBC polling points to a potential “toss-up” between the Democratic and Republican parties.

Former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, the Democratic contender, is campaigning on affordability, healthcare access, education funding, and environmental regulation. Her campaign says she aims to “deliver for working families and bring steady leadership to Georgia in the midst of uncertainty and chaos coming from Washington”.

If she wins, she would become the first black woman elected governor in the US.

Bottoms is up against 72-year-old billionaire Rick Jackson, who has accused her of failing to deal with crime during her tenure as Atlanta mayor.

Jackson has spent more than $200m of his own money on advertisements featuring demonstrations and violence in Atlanta following the killing of Rayshard Brooks , an unarmed black man, by a white Atlanta police officer in 2020. The killing happened while Bottoms was Atlanta mayor.

Americans have been voting for weeks, with 40 million ballots already cast, according to the University of Florida’s election lab. A total of 45.9 million Americans voted early in the last midterm elections in 2022.

articles.title: Trump snaps at reporter asking about his health
articles.summary: President Trump on Thursday snapped at a reporter asked a question about whether his recent rally cancellations were related to his health or being sick of traveling. Trump was originally scheduled to travel to Salina, Kan., over the weekend to rally voters for Republican candidates, days ahead of the midterm elections. His in-person visit was…
articles.body:
President Trump on Thursday snapped at a reporter asked a question about whether his recent rally cancellations were related to his health or being sick of traveling.

Trump was originally scheduled to travel to Salina, Kan., over the weekend to rally voters for Republican candidates, days ahead of the midterm elections. His in-person visit was cancelled and replaced by a series of telerallies in multiple states , including Kansas and Iowa.

After the changes were announced, a reporter from Reuters pressed the president on the decision. A video clip of the interaction, posted by PBS News , shows Trump saying he has been doing “good” while on the campaign trail.

The journalist followed up with another inquiry about his health, as he has been doing “a lot of traveling.”

“Oh, you’re sick to ask that question. You are sick,” Trump replied.

“You’ve been following me for two weeks. I feel perfect. You are disgusting,” he continued. “Put yourself in shape. You look like hell.”

Kansas is home to one of the high-stakes Senate races that could help determine control of the upper chamber next year. Incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall (R) is facing a tough battle against Democratic candidate Adam Hamilton.

Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ rates the contest as leaning narrowly in favor of Marshall, who has a 58 percent probability of winning.

Trump told reporters that while he opted for a telerally in the Sunflower State instead of traveling Saturday, “he is doing very well.” The president reminded the reporter that he will still be traveling Friday for a campaign event in Florida.

“I don’t feel I have to go to Kansas, I’m going to Florida tomorrow,” he said.

This is not the first time the president has snapped at a reporter in recent days. Earlier this month, he cut off a reporter in the Oval Office that started to ask about the East Potomac Park golf course renovations and subsequent legal battle .

“What’s wrong with you? Are you a sick person?” the president added.

articles.title: China denies allegations of spy operation targeting Nvidia CEO
articles.summary: US intelligence officials believe a Chinese businesswoman was gathering information for Beijing on the US chip-making giant, The New York Times reports.
articles.body:
China has rejected allegations of a Chinese espionage operation targeting Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang, describing the claims as "groundless speculation".

US intelligence officials believe that Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman linked to Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed, was gathering information for Beijing on the US chip-making giant, according to a report by The New York Times .

The report said Alice Huang, who is of no relation to Jensen Huang, was under investigation over the possible diversion of advanced Nvidia AI chips to China and had developed a close relationship with Jensen.

Nvidia said their interactions were routine business engagements, while Beijing accused Washington of attempting to smear China. Alice Huang did not respond to the paper's request for comment.

The BBC has contacted Megaspeed and the White House for comment.

US intelligence agencies had been monitoring Alice Huang and concluded that she was acting on behalf of the Chinese government, according to unnamed sources cited by The New York Times.

Surveillance reportedly revealed communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, who was subsequently identified as Jensen Huang through a process known as "unmasking".

It remains unclear what information Alice Huang - who is also known as Huang Le - allegedly passed to Beijing, how valuable it was, or when she is believed to have begun gathering intelligence.

At a regular briefing on Friday, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said: "The report in question is based on groundless speculation and is nothing more than an attempt to smear China."

The paper's report comes amid longstanding US concerns about China's access to advanced computing technology, which is considered crucial to developing artificial intelligence systems.

Jensen Huang has argued that allowing Nvidia to sell more of its products to China is important for maintaining US competitiveness in the global AI industry.

But Washington has restricted exports of the most advanced Nvidia chips to China since 2022, citing national security concerns and the risk that the technology could strengthen China's military operations. There have however been some loosening of restrictions during Trump's administration.

US officials said they had caught several firms illegally trafficking the chips across the Chinese border. They have also investigated whether companies operating through third countries are helping Chinese businesses access the restricted technology.

Nvidia has said it complies with applicable export laws and that there is no evidence its chips have been smuggled into China.

In response to the allegations made by the Times, John Rizzo, a spokesman for Nvidia, said: "Jensen's interactions with Ms Huang are not unusual or unexpected".

He said customers like Megaspeed "receive ordinary business information - not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets - and zero information relevant to national security."

He added that allegations the Singaporean company was smuggling chips to China "were thoroughly investigated and debunked last year".

Megaspeed told the paper its current leadership took the allegations seriously and had appointed external legal advisers to conduct an internal investigation. The company also said it had informed the US government that it was willing to cooperate.

It is unclear how closely Alice Huang remains involved with Megaspeed.

articles.title: Peltola insists 'I knew nothing' about alleged 'Decoy Dan' scheme as Sullivan alleges she is 'still lying'
articles.summary: Mary Peltola claims she "knew nothing" about the alleged scheme to recruit candidates named Dan Sullivan, but the incumbent says she is "still lying."
articles.body: Alaska Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola insisted she "knew nothing" about an alleged scheme to recruit people with the same name as her opponent to run in the election, while incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan told Fox News she is "still lying." "I just want to clear the air," Peltola began in a speech to supporters on Thursday in Juneau. "I knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about. I am not interested in tricking voters. I know I can beat Dan Sullivan." In an interview with Fox News, Sullivan, a Republican, said Peltola's campaign "demonstrated the most corrupt action you could take." "Most candidates, when they run for office, I've run for office, and this is my third election. You sit down at the beginning of your election with your advisers to think about 'What's my record? I'm going to run on a strong record. What's my vision? What do I want to get done?' Peltola sat down with her advisers, Democrats from D.C. and Alaska, and their first order of business was 'how do we cheat? How do we make sure Alaskans throw away their votes?'" Sullivan said. "This was a secret project that they had. And then they worked on it for over a year. And then she consistently lied about it. What's amazing to me is how consistently and casually everyone involved in this, from Kirsten Gillibrand and Schumer down to Peltola and her advisors, and everybody in between lied about this directly to the Alaskan people," Sullivan continued. "Heck, Peltola is still lying about it, right?" SEN DAN SULLIVAN BRANDS PELTOLA’S ALLEGED BALLOT SCHEME A ‘SCANDAL AT THE HIGHEST ORDER’ The New York Times reported Wednesday that Peltola’s campaign, as well as senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, carried out the alleged election scheme in hopes that voters would be confused by two Dan Sullivans and therefore draw support from the incumbent Republican senator. The Justice Department is moving to delay certification of Alaska’s U.S. Senate election results since two individuals by the name of Dan Sullivan appear alongside each other on the ballot. The state’s incumbent U.S. senator is listed on the ballot as "Sullivan, Dan S.," while the other Dan Sullivan, a retired schoolteacher, is listed as "Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr." The latter is known to his critics as "Decoy Dan." PELTOLA CAMPAIGN'S ALLEGED DAN SULLIVAN SPOILER PLOT TAKES NEW TURN AS DOJ FACES MAJOR LEGAL HURDLE Sen. Sullivan told Fox News correspondent Matt Finn that what he is hearing on the campaign trail is "the disdain that this shows that Peltola has for the Alaskan people." "Think about it. Her first big move as a candidate, she hadn't announced her candidacy yet, was to rig the system and work together to cheat and to recruit a candidate whose sole purpose, we all know now, was to confuse Alaskans to rig the vote for her. It is a shocker. It's the biggest scandal in Alaskan electoral history by far," Sullivan said. articles.body:
President Trump is making one more in-person midterm push in the Sunshine State on Friday, a day after the Republican National Committee announced he was scratching his weekend rallies in Kansas and Iowa.

Trump is set to speak in Daytona Beach, Fla., around 7 p.m. to vouch for Sen. Ashley Moody (R) in her race against Rep. Angie Nixon (D) and gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds (R) in his highly contested battle against Democrat David Jolly.

The president will hold tele-rallies this weekend in Texas, Kansas, Iowa, New York, Pennsylvania, Michigan, Montana and South Carolina.

It’s a big day in court Friday in Washington as well. The fight over East Potomac Park ‘s golf course returns to court at 10 a.m., with Judge Ana Reyes having ordered a new hearing regarding Trump’s plans for the site after he posted on social media this week vowing to press ahead despite her ruling halting it.

At 11 a.m., former FBI Director James Comey appears in court, where his attorneys will press for the judge to dismiss the Justice Department’s third criminal case against him.
